The model works by identifying the optimal combination of kernels and amounts to produce a high-quality restored image from degraded input. The model's performance surpasses the current state-of-the-art in denoising and deblurring real-world images and also achieves impressive results in synthetic tests.

We introduce a novel type of algebraic structure called a multipermutable loop of $G$-sets that builds upon the concept of a multipermutable quasigroup. Our analysis shows that the set of all multipermutable loops forms a variety that can be defined through specific equations. Furthermore, we establish that the category of multipermutable loops is equivalent to the category of uniform groups satisfying a specific $G$-action-related $\delta$-deformation. Additionally, we present an application involving yield matrices tied to the notional quasigroups of Kirkman groups and extended van Kampen groups.

Formal verification through Hoare logic is a proven method, but its practical limitation lies in manually crafting detailed specification conditions for each program, a task that many find too laborious and impractical. In contrast, natural language specifications of programs are easily understood but challenging to formalize. This paper proposes an approach that enables program verification based on natural language descriptions through the incorporation of Natural Hoare Reasoning. This method enables the formal verification of a program using a specification derived directly from its natural language description, thus reducing the labor required for formal verification. The effectiveness of this approach is dependent on advancing both natural language understanding and formal verification, necessitating a unified framework for formal specification. This paper describes a preliminary framework for this purpose and reports on its application to a real-world program.

This research introduces RCanopus, a novel and robust consensus network that handles failures and malicious interventions efficiently. RCanopus builds upon the consensus protocol of Canopus, a highly reliable and low-latency system previously developed. RCanopus, in contrast, focuses on tackling a particular type of fault, known as the variable failure fault, in a consensus protocol. It is characterized by an unknown number of failing nodes producing conflicting views. Our work undertakes the first instance of designing a consensus protocol capable of withstanding variable failure faults without assuming a fixed failure rate. RCanopus is grounded in a fundamental study of a particular type of low-latency consensus protocol, known as bag-of-tricks (BoT), which is designed with resilience to temporary network partitions in mind. It is notable, however, that BoT fails to meet all criteria for producing stable consensus outcomes on its own. Our research extends upon this foundation by combining BoT with two novel components, known as CheckGC and DLR-CheckGC, to guarantee failure resiliency in RCanopus without relying on time-consuming and expensive failure detection mechanisms. RCanopus achieves this system-level resiliency in just three message exchanges and covers all of its message exchanges under a uniform bound. It is capable of withstanding up to C+1 failures at any given time, where C represents the fixed failure rate assuming no additional failures. Furthermore, RCanopus is future-proof and can accommodate an increasing failure rate without any modification. Our

Recent studies using neutron spin echo and X-ray spectroscopy have found that membranes containing cholesterol exhibit an irregularity in their movement that contradicts the expected random fluctuation in their shape. Although this abnormality is relatively small, it needs to be explored further to determine its relationship with the presence of cholesterol. To assist in the interpretation of the experimental results, a detailed simulation of the lipid bilayer movement is presented, using a model that includes the effects of both cholesterol and the experimental conditions. This simulation reveals that the unusual fluctuation in the bilayer's curvature can be accurately represented by a single parameter characterizing the bilayer's elasticity. With this parameter, we can assess a characteristic time for the bilayer's deformation and compare it with existing measurements, while also considering the impact of cholesterol on the bilayer's structure.

Developing a new model for very dense and compact stars based on Loop Quantum Gravity theory's ADM representation is our goal. This model is formed by selecting suitable scale factors for the spatial and temporal metrics, which are then used to define a modified stress-energy tensor.  In this study, we examine the influence of gravity constraints resulting from the ADM representation on the stress-energy tensor. Furthermore, we investigate how loop quantum gravity corrections to the metric influence neutron stars and black holes.  Specifically, we are interested in understanding how these corrections affect the density and pressure at the core of these objects, as well as their impact on the radius of hypothetical supermassive black holes with masses similar to those described by the M\o ch-Kerr metric.

The catalog of most energetic cosmic rays recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory up to date covers 25 years of operation, from 2004 to 2009, during which the observatory detected 33 events exceeding 50 EeV. This collection includes data on the energy, location, depth of the atmosphere at observation height, proton and helium rates, overall uncertainty, and associated uncertainties of the highest-energy particles detected in the southern hemisphere, along with comparisons to comparable events observed in the northern hemisphere by the Telescope Array. This extensive review examines the distribution of energy, arrival directions, and depth of the atmosphere at observation height for both the proton and helium compositions of the most energetic particles observed. This study also provides an estimate of an energetic particle's relative probability based on its energy, arrival direction, and depth of the atmosphere at observation height represented by a function. Moreover, the document compares the energies measured by the Pierre Auger Observatory and Telescope Array for each of the 25 most energetic events, with values differing by 7% or less. Finally, the document presents a summary of the observatory's energetic events, including an assessment of the uncertainty in the composition and depth of the atmosphere at observation height for each of the 25 most energetic events, with compositions analyzed using the Lukas-Morstam method and both the anthropogenic and cosmogenic neutrino fluxes calculated.

Incorporating uncertainty information into deep neural network-based object detectors enhances their reliability and robustness. This research introduces BayesOD, a lightweight object detector that accurately captures its classification and regression uncertainties. The design comprises two key components: firstly, replacing the traditional CuDNN K-means++ algorithm with a Bayesian method for initializing the cluster centers of anchor boxes. The second element involves utilising the variational inference-based mean-field objective function to optimise the odds and confidence loss weights. Evaluations of the proposed BayesOD on the COCO and ICCV datasets demonstrate its uncertainties to be well-validatable and consistently more accurate than existing approaches. Furthermore, this study develops a straightforward and efficient approach for assessing the uncertainty of object detectors.

The prediction of traffic flow is a significant issue in the transportation science field. The development of microscopic traffic prediction models from satellite imagery has emerged as a promising approach, leveraging machine learning algorithms to identify segment-level predictions from image-based data. Despite this, existing solutions are limited by their reliance on accurate segment boundaries, a condition often not met in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we introduce a new framework for traffic prediction, centered on predicting segment assignments in advance. The framework consists of two key models, focusing on predicting both speed and route assignments, each operating at different scales. The network architecture for the speed-predicting model involves a Hierarchy of Transformer-based Attention Modifiers, enhancing the performance of the transformer encoder and enabling efficient use of the historical traffic data. Furthermore, we propose a new approach to estimating the distribution of moving segments from observations, leveraging a power-by-exponentiation strategy to enable robust segment-based predictions. The proposed scheme was evaluated using a dataset of approximately 500,000 traffic instances and nearly 18 million images, demonstrating improved accuracy and efficiency over existing solutions. The introduced methods and implemented code have been made publicly available to facilitate replication of these findings.

In the context of rewriting Boolean functions via norm-based techniques, the concept of Gray equivalence emerges as a pivotal tool for analyzing rewriting methods in multiple norms and comparing their efficacy in various scenarios. We utilize Gray equivalence to develop a crucial consistency test, which enables the evaluation of rewriting methods across diverse norms without in-depth knowledge of the underlying basis. This consistency test can be applied in three primary domains, namely norm rewriting, Boolean decision procedures, and Knuth-Bendix completion, with far-reaching implications in each area. We focus on two main applications within these domains, namely rewriting Boolean functions without integers and Boolean decision procedures via rewriting methods. With the help of Gray equivalence, we develop a set of necessary conditions for integer coefficients equivalent to unit leading one vectors, thereby providing a set of sufficient conditions for zero equivalence in integer matrices with a focus on rewriting methods. These conditions are instrumental in understanding when unit leading one vectors can be achieved through rewriting methods. Additionally, we show that the existing Gray rewriting method does not fully capture the set of equivalent leading vectors, thereby prompting the development of new rewriting methods. Lastly, we examine the methodological implications of our Gray equivalence-based approach and its consistency test.

An AI technique identifying hippocampal alterations in brain MR images has been developed to diagnose epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. Two CNN architectures were combined and evaluated for their performance, effectively distinguishing hippocampal changes caused by epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease, and normal hippocampal development. The employed method outperformed a baseline classification model, achieving a 92% accuracy rate. This novel approach utilizing MR imaging enables early detection of hippocampal abnormalities and contributes to both epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.

In an interferometer with many components, even if the input contains a specific number of distinct frequencies, inherent system properties will cause a spreading effect such that none of the output frequencies will be missing, a phenomenon resulting from the inherent diversity of transversal modes within the system. This phenomenon is more effectively illustrated by using an unsuppressed multi-frequency signal within an attenuating system rather than a resonating one. Furthermore, to assess the influence of data loss on this phenomenon, an alternative approach is proposed, in which the amount of missing output frequency is treated as a measurable quantity.

Our research focuses on modeling the capture of Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) particles at low Earth orbiting satellites. The primary goal is to establish a relationship between the rates at which neutrons are detected inside a satellite and the cosmic ray fluxes reaching the Earth's atmosphere, particularly focusing on protons and electrons. Our model's initial assessment suggests that while neutrons captured by satellites are largely produced by cosmic ray protons, the electrons' contribution to this process is surprisingly significant, particularly at low latitudes. This finding has important implications for experimental data analysis related to neutrons.

A comprehensive design framework for Deep Graph Neural Networks is proposed, incorporating a multi-stage learning approach that integrates global and local neighbourhood information through spatial and temporal adaptations. The framework leverages a Pyramid-like Shrinkage Pyramid, leveraging pre-built graphs, and incorporates Reconfiguration Operators to dynamically adjust edge connections based on node health scores and neighbourhood regularity. The framework also incorporates a novel Topology-aware optimizer for efficient parameter selection, and a comprehensive model selection system that evaluates model performance and reliability. The proposed framework is demonstrated through a range of experimental applications, including weather forecasting, plant phenotyping, and healthcare decision support, showcasing its versatility and adaptability in addressing diverse challenges.

To safeguard sensitive information in low-rank matrices, various techniques are employed, such as differential privacy. A specific method, known as low-rank matrix fulfillment (LRMF), utilizes low-rank matrix completion to achieve private low-rank matrices. Notably, there are two primary forms of robustness required for an LRMF mechanism: global sensitivity-related privacy and local privacy. A specific mechanism, known as the "smoothed singular value thresholding" algorithm, is used in literature to offer private low-rank matrices. This algorithm, known as its DS-SVST form, is able to provide only global sensitivity-based privacy. This study proposes a new form of DS-SVST, known as its d-SVST form, to offer private low-rank matrices using local privacy. Additionally, it presents a new form of DS-SVST, known as its w-SVST form, to offer warm-started estimates that are superior in terms of accuracy to d-SVST. Through mathematical analysis and experiments, it was demonstrated that d-SVST form offers significantly better privacy-utility trade-off compared to previous mechanisms.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust that incorporates different components and their optical properties more accurately than previous models. This new model reveals that a standard type of dust (PAHs) is sufficient to account for most of the observed polarization and emission of light from galaxies. Other dust components, specifically smaller particles and a type of dust called CNs, also produce observable effects but are less dominant. The new model not only improves our understanding of interstellar dust but also provides a tool for extracting detailed information about the distribution and properties of dust in the universe from observations of different wavelengths and angles.

The object CIDA 1 lies at the lowest end of the mass range of stars and has a significant coronal emission, which makes it easily detectable. It has a disk with characteristics similar to those of higher-mass stars, and a sub-mm observation has revealed the presence of a massive planet. We used the ALMA telescope to obtain a higher resolution image of the CIDA 1 disk and its surrounding environment. Our analysis suggests that the massive planet has a mass of about 2.3 times the mass of Jupiter. This planet likely formed in the disk and may have induced the absence of CO emission by exhausting its gas through mechanisms such as photo-evaporation, sending the gas to higher altitudes, or both. Observing stars with a mass similar to CIDA 1 but more massive can help confirm whether this phenomenon is unique to low-mass stars and can shed light on the process of planet formation.

The Lights Out game is a well-known online game where the goal is to solve a given instance by sequence of clicks on lights. Research on this game has led to a model called the Maximum Stimulus Model (MSM), which represents the most efficient strategy for solving the Lights Out game. A recent issue with this model is that it may not always result in the maximum number of clicks needed to solve the instance. We have developed a new model, the Maximum Stimulus Model with Conflict (MSMC), based on MSM, to address this limitation. By comparing MSM and MSMC, we have shown that MSMC can identify whether an instance is solvable and, if so, determine the maximum number of clicks needed to solve it. Additionally, we have outlined the process for converting any instance of the Lights Out game into an instance of the Extended Deadlock Paradox, a problem of integer optimization, and explained how solving the latter would yield the maximum number of clicks required to solve the former. Furthermore, we have proposed an algorithm (Lights Out Algorithm, LOA) for solving MSMC instances, which works by integrating elements from the Maximum Stimulus Model and Conflict Resolution, and demonstrated its applicability to generalizations of the Lights Out game, such as the Circular Lights Out game (CLO) and the Invertible Lights Out game (ILO). Experimental results have shown that LOA is more efficient than the standard MSM, another recent algorithm due to Bragin (2019).

This paper presents an innovative image partitioning model inspired by the Donoho-Talagrand model for sparse signals. We derive this model by applying the principle of variance minimization to images in different sub-spaces. To overcome the model's complexity resulting from the vast number of possible sub-spaces, we introduce a new convex formulation of the model. We develop an efficient algorithm for solving this formulation, achieving a balance between the number of partitions and image reconstruction quality. We also introduce a model selection method that simultaneously determines the number of partitions and the parameters of the model. We evaluate the effectiveness of our model by applying it to synthetic and real-world images, achieving excellent results in terms of partition quality and image reconstruction. Compared to the Donoho-Talagrand model, our model has a significant improvement in computational efficiency without sacrificing partition quality.

To enhance the accuracy of abstract interpretation, a novel abstraction technique known as Forward Abstraction Delayed Simulation (FADS) has been proposed. FADS aims to identify the most critical time to abstract data for each program point by analyzing its simulation throughout different levels of abstraction. A key aspect of FADS is its ability to adjust the abstraction level in real-time, allowing for a more precise simulation. We have also developed SimRL, a general framework for verifying the safety of deep reinforcement learning agents in a real-time environment. Through case studies on various applications, it was proven that FADS can frequently determine the required abstraction level much earlier than traditional methods, resulting in a more efficient simulation and more accurate results.

We have theoretically identified and analyzed a class of topological phonons in
solid-state devices, specifically in ferroelectric ceramic materials, and shown
that their characteristics can be adjusted by using the phenomenon of strain
photomutation. The topological phonons in these ceramics produce pure spin
currents without accompanying charge currents, and, due to their unique
properties, may possess two types of topological features simultaneously. The
phases of the rotating strain and temperature are crucial factors influencing
the quantum properties of the phonon system, and, as a result, the phonon
properties can be regulated selectively through temperature or light manipulation.

Identifying irregular patterns in data is crucial for many applications. However, detecting outliers in high-dimensional spaces with complex structures is challenging due to the poor accuracy and performance issues associated with existing methods. To address this problem, we propose a new method that builds on graph theory and nearest neighbor search. By employing a nearest neighbor graph, our method efficiently detects outliers based on the consistency of the local geometry. Experimental results across various datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses other techniques in both accuracy and processing time. To further facilitate outlier detection, we develop an open-source Python library incorporating our proposed approach and also provide a comprehensive comparison with the existing state-of-the-art techniques using standardized benchmarks.

We analyze how a Clarence-Mond quantum atom reacts when faced with a smooth,
fixed mirror and subjected to external stimulation at a specific frequency.
Our research reveals that this atom's movement can lead to excitation and the
emission of light, similar to how light is emitted when the atom interacts with
an oscillating mirror. Additionally, we investigate how varying parameters like
movement speed, traction, and stimulation intensity affects both forms of light
emission - one caused by excitation and the other by the atom's slippage. In a
further exploration, we study the characteristics of light emitted from the atom
when it slips past the mirror using a classical method and find that this slippage
can produce electromagnetic waves with polarizations that range from linear to
elliptical in shape.

Graph convolution networks exhibit biases that manifest as node attribute variations depending on the chosen kernel type - an issue that limits their effectiveness and reliability when working with unlabelled data. To address this problem, we developed a method that adjusts graph convolutions to prioritize fairness in the resulting node attributes by incorporating neighborhood diversity into the convolution operation. By measuring the difference between subgraphs and applying a straightforward weight normalization, we ensure that the modified convolution learns the mean of each feature dimension to achieve equality. Additionally, we modified the backpropagation mechanism to distribute fairness errors to edge weights, enabling our method to capture group-level patterns. To demonstrate its applicability to unsupervised tasks, we used our method with a semi-supervised node classification framework, considering both static and dynamic neighbourhoods. Experiment results on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that incorporating fairness effectively eliminates colour bias in GCNs, with the potential to further identify underlying group-level patterns through optimal edge weights.

To analyze the dynamics of reversible enzyme reactions, we employ the Kurchan-Martin-Landau-Semenoff model. This model is a Planck-Firsov-Khristoforov model modified to account for reversibility. Our goal is to develop an iterative solution for the kinetic equations describing the reaction's temporal evolution, particularly in the steady state. This investigation is crucial as the iterative solution yields an approximation that is as accurate as the fully analytical solution when the iteration is infinite. To extract a meaningful approximation, an intrinsic characteristic time scale needs to be identified, which separates kinetic events from measurements.

Theoretical models incorporating supersymmetry, specifically two distinct types where its impact is either evident in particle physics or hidden, were examined for collisions involving a proton and a proton at an energy of 13 TeV, focusing on events containing multiple jets and a notable absence of momentum. These models include manifest supersymmetry, a supergravity model with a universally abundant scalar, and the WIMPless supersymmetry, which involves two distinct types where its impact is either evident in particle physics or hidden, were examined for collisions involving a proton and a proton at an energy of 13 TeV, focusing on events containing multiple jets and a notable absence of momentum. Events consistent with containing a graviton or scalar particle were analyzed for their relevance using simplified models. As a result, even with data volumes as small as 36 inverse femtobarns, various distinct supersymmetry models with particles having masses up to 1000 GeV were shown to be excluded. Similarly, even with data volumes as small as 36 inverse femtobarns, various distinct supersymmetry models with particles having masses up to 1000 GeV were shown to be excluded.

This research investigates financial bubbles in complex systems of interconnected expectational models linked to random variables with stochastic termination times. The study assumes mean-reverting tendencies in these agents' expectations, supported by empirical evidence. The research considers scenarios involving both interdependent agent expectations and a shared factor driving their perceptions. The analysis utilizes tools from non-linear differential equations and stochastic processes to examine the dynamics of agent expectations, focusing on their behavior at critical points of sudden change. The study evaluates bubbles based on their critical point features and duration, and provides quantitative assessments using metrics such as the Cram\'{e}r exponent and the Cvetkovic-Nikolic quantity. The research also delves into the collective behavior of agents with shared stimuli, demonstrating that even minor interactions between participants can lead to the disappearance of critical points and major impacts on bubble duration.

This study examines the utilization of Markov-Chain Monte Carlo methods in analyzing the characteristics of a driven harmonic oscillator under specific conditions where it is coupled with a bath of oscillators. Two primary models are investigated: a specific scenario in which there is no energy exchange with the bath, and another more complex scenario in which energy exchange does occur. In the first scenario, which is more manageable, Monte Carlo techniques enable the derivation of an exact effective Hamiltonian describing the behavior of a driven oscillator in its vicinity. In the second, more intricate scenario, which involves energy exchange with the bath, Monte Carlo techniques allow the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian that describes the behavior of a driven harmonic oscillator, which has a specific broadening to its resonance. These findings may have significant broader implications for the analysis of diverse systems.

In product recommendation tasks, particularly when relying on reviews, combining both direct and indirect information is crucial for accurate outcomes. Existing research suggests combining review features with user-item interaction data can greatly improve performance, yet this approach often overlooks the sensitive relationship between reviews and user reactions. We propose a novel model called Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which efficiently handles review features and user-item interactions through a unified framework by using a sentiment-related channel to merge information. Experimental results confirm that SIFN significantly surpasses baseline models in both real-world datasets and top-ranked Kaggle competitions. Additionally, the underlying reason for its success, namely the sentiment-sensitive information fusion, has also been visually demonstrated.

This study investigates data augmentation techniques for CS AR-EN text sequences by evaluating the effectiveness of lexical substitution methods on improved language modeling performance. Two techniques are specifically examined: replacing each word in a sentence with a synonym, and selecting a single replacement word based on co-occurrence in a parallel corpus. These methods were applied to CS AR-EN text data and led to notable gains in perplexity scores, with the highest improvements achieved on an EN-AR CS language model, reaching up to 23% lower than the baseline.

We show that any subgroup of surface diffeomorphisms whose action on the sphere is non-wild is relatively compact in the Roelcke topology, but this property fails for subgroups of diffeomorphisms with arbitrarily large topological degree of transfer. Additionally, we identify the exact threshold above which such subgroups become relatively compact in the topology of uniform convergence.

A new approach, the connectable state, is proposed for branes at generalised orbifold fixed points, using a layer-by-layer construction. It is shown that a regularised Witten spin connection compatible with the jump operators of the lambda model can be used across all layers, thereby enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the open string spectrum through the bulk topological string theory. For certain lambda deformations of type IIA/IB models, it is demonstrated that a regularised six-dimensional spin connection compatible with the twist and spin connection of the Lee-Rozjankowski model can be used, thereby recovering the regularised seven-dimensional spin connection of the untwisted model when the deformation parameter vanishes.

Higher-quality and complex visualizations in rendering and animation rely heavily on hexahedral meshes, which offer several benefits including improved topology and enhanced data retrieval. However, creating these meshes can be a complex and time-consuming process involving multiple algorithms and different topological operators. To address this issue, a novel extension has been proposed that allows mesh editors to create large-scale meshes consisting of up to 58 tets per hex element. This extension overcomes the limitation of a single tet building block by allowing the insertion of various tetrahedra, but due to the resulting increased complexity, it also introduces new constraints and limitations to prevent excessive computational overhead. Specifically, this approach imposes a hard limit on the total number of tets in the mesh, as well as a soft limit based on the mesh's overall quality metrics, to prevent performance degradation due to the added overhead. Additionally, this proposed method utilizes a non-trivial cost function to optimize the quality of the resulting meshes by incorporating quality-related constraints. As a result, it outperforms alternative topological operators in terms of quality, while also offering improved efficiency and speed. To implement this innovative approach, a new operator is described, along with its underlying principles and limitations, offering a practical solution for creating high-quality hex meshes.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common objective of establishing connections between entities within a graph.
Building upon this similarity, we investigate how to leverage link prediction
models to enhance relation extraction, and demonstrate this synergy through an
novel approach which integrates a relation extraction task with a weakened
version of the head-tail alignment component of the head-tail alignment-based
link prediction model. Experimental results indicate that this synergy leads to
improved performance in relation extraction. Furthermore, we utilize the link
prediction model to create negative samples for training, which in turn yields
higher accuracy and increased F1-score for the integrated relation extraction task.

To optimize the performance of an analytical delay model for use in circuit design, we develop a personal core library of mathematical functions for delay analysis. This library leverages Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolkit to incorporate different types of delay models with varying assumptions. The purpose of this core library is to ensure consistency in the core models and facilitate their incorporation into the analytical delay models in the widely used Cadence SoC Encounter tool. One of the delay models we model is the converter delay, which occurs when signals transition from CMOS to the reliable but slower magnetic domain. This phenomenon arises from the magnetic oxide breakdown caused by high current flow, leading to signal disruptions and significant delay. The magnetic domain is particularly sensitive to temperature, and as temperature rises, signal integrity degrades and delay increases. The converter delay model we developed is based on a power law incorporating factors for threshold, bias, temperature, and the physical properties of the magnetic oxide.

In the realm of reinforcement learning, utilizing continuity helps facilitate the transfer of learned knowledge between slightly modified environments.  However, continuing the learning process in metric spaces proves challenging due to their nature of having infinitely many nearby points.  Prior research, mainly focusing on highly structured manifolds, has yielded limited insights for the broader class of metric spaces.  We have successfully developed a novel continuity condition tailored for reinforcement learning, applicable to a wide range of metric spaces, and it encompasses multiple existing continuity conditions.  Moreover, our research demonstrates that our condition minimizes the assumptions required for transfer learning, while also highlighting instances where prior approaches fail.  Theoretical validations and empirical experiments confirm the expected benefits of our continuity condition.

Previous research has demonstrated the ability to detect the animacy of objects from various aspects, but the internal workings of this process remain unclear. To determine the essential characteristics contributing to animacy perception, we conducted an experiment where subjects evaluated the animacy of images and identified the key factors through regression analysis. This revealed that face and body presence, as well as certain contextual elements (such as eyes and a head), significantly influence animacy judgment. Subsequently, we examined how neurological responses in the ventral temporal brain area, as activated by the presence of animatable features, varied in relation to the detected animacy level. Notably, we discovered distinct neural patterns in response to animacy judgments, regardless of the actual presence or absence of animatable features, further characterizing the animacy structure in this brain region. This research was subsequently extended to electrical stimulation studies within the brain, which provided new insights into the animacy processing mechanism and raised essential and thought-provoking inquiries regarding the animacy structure, such as whether animacy is an objective property and how animacy is subjectively perceived by individuals.

Multidimensional problems solved using the finite element method can have precise numerical solutions, but these solutions are often obstructed by numerical errors resulting in an unwanted arrangement of solution values. Arrangements, comprising convex/half-space regions where specific value combinations occur, are typically disregarded in the reference solution due to being non-physical or negligible. In industrial contexts, where spatial detail is crucial, overlooking these regions can lead to crucial data being missed. To address this issue, a new filter was developed, one that ensures no arrangement values are lost within the output. The proposed filter relies on a convex optimization component which identifies and protects arrangement regions. It achieves this by placing a convex hull over local hyperplane arrangements and uses l1-regularization to keep iterations on the moving hull. The filter was successfully applied to two FD and FE-based problems and demonstrated to accurately preserve arrangement-based data within the output solution.

We investigate the spatial characteristics of the corona surrounding the black hole candidate, IGR J12346-5124, by studying the X-ray observations of the MAXI J1535-571, recorded by the Insight-HXMT. Our findings reveal that resonance scattering occurs between the quasi-periodic fluctuations type C and the soft X-ray photons, yielding distinct spatial corona patterns. Observations indicate that the inner corona spatial extent spans from the black hole's Schwarzschild radius to its iron absorption feature and that this structure changes over time, influencing the inner boundary's position. Consequently, on day 229, it appears that the inner boundary lies entirely within the Schwarzschild radius. Moreover, our findings show that on day 231, the inner boundary spans from the Schwarzschild radius to its iron absorption feature and that this structure changes over time, influencing the inner boundary's position. Consequently, on day 231, it appears that the inner boundary spans from the Schwarzschild radius to its iron absorption feature and that this structure changes over time, influencing the inner boundary's position.

In multi-agent autonomous systems, agents are expected to autonomously make decisions and engage in proactive actions. To achieve this, they need to be designed with internal drive and motivation. Our approach, known as transfer empowerment, introduces an innovative method for training autonomous entities. We show that by minimizing the variability in an agent's perceived control over its surroundings, empowered agents naturally develop a internal desire to interact and respond to their partners in a more anticipatory and adaptive manner. This framework is rooted in information-theoretic principles and facilitates social behavior without requiring external reward structures or explicit instruction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of transfer empowerment through its applications in both simulated and real-world settings, such as online chess tutorials and human-robot interaction. Our research reveals that empowered agents exhibit socially relevant behaviors, including self-initiated action, awareness of partner's behavioral capabilities, tolerance for delay in response, and detection of partner's behavioral changes. Moreover, we find that transfer empowerment enables robots to seamlessly adapt to new human interactions and provide helpful responses, as validated by subjective human assessments.

We introduce Contrastive Learning with Physics-based Simulation (CLPS), a data-efficient technique that can identify any unknown substance given a spectral observation using physics-based rendering. By training a single CLPS model on multiple tasks, we successfully simulate and replicate the spectral observations of diverse substances. Our method achieves this by employing a shared CLPS model that learns a universal subspace spanning a range of substances, allowing it to accurately identify unknown substances regardless of their composition, conditions, or configuration, as long as they fall within the learned subspace. Building on the CLPS framework, we successfully tested and demonstrated the CLPS method in a range of scenarios, such as simulating various substances, conditions, and configurations, and we hope that our method will serve as a useful foundation for tackling challenging spectral identification tasks in various areas of applied physics, such as material identification, astrophysics, and planetary science, where a comprehensive database may not be available.

Two equivalent definitions of a Lie 2-algebra, a type of multi-dimensional algebra, are examined in detail. The definition is elaborated upon by considering an associated 2-term chain complex, and key examples of Lie 2-algebras are provided, along with some foundational theorems including adaptions of Baer's theorem. The article delves into Lie 2-algebra homomorphisms and shows how a form of decomposition similar to decomposition into irreducible parts applies. Moreover, the article discusses cohomology related to Lie 2-algebras and begins to explore the broader Lie 2-algebra cone, incorporating topics such as infinitesimal Lie 2-algebras and 2-derivative algebras.

We introduce a detector-free object matching approach, suited for robust
real-world applications of pose tracking and scene understanding. Our novel
method, LoFTR, leverages a hierarchical local feature matching strategy that
enables efficient and precise object position estimation, even on challenging
visual tasks. Additionally, we present an optimized method for dense feature
matching across different scales, enabling our approach to reach a remarkable
95.7\% average accuracy on the benchmark dataset NTU RGB+D. Our proposed
method also demonstrates superior performance on the human pose dataset
Human3.6M. Moreover, we present a method for using our approach on unseen
objects solely based on their pose, effectively enabling transfer learning.
Furthermore, we present a method for cross-cultural pose estimation, where
our approach can accurately identify and track poses across different
cultures, even on limited data, solely based on pose, resulting in a 6% gain
on average.

The construction of a comprehensive solar magnetic field map relies on combining multiple observations of the solar vector magnetic field from various telescopes. Since it's impossible to map the entire Sun's surface with data from current telescopes, we rely on computer models to fill in the gaps. However, these models can introduce biases that negatively impact the quality of the map. In order to identify and minimize these biases, we developed two key techniques. Firstly, we created a metric that identifies biased data points based on the magnetic field values they produce. Secondly, we employed an iterative process that uses the collective information from all data points to refine and correct the magnetic field predictions. By using this approach, we were able to significantly improve the accuracy of magnetic field predictions for test datasets.

A major obstacle to utilizing load control methods on consumers is the considerable cost associated with load control, which necessitates advanced demand response systems to effectively manage this trade-off between benefits and costs for both aggregators and individual consumers. To address this challenge, this research introduces a new independent demand side control approach that incorporates a two-stage game theory model. The approach separates demand response into two components, load forecasting and real-time load management, which are optimized using planned load charging and variable load charging, respectively. The proposed method can reduce the overall cost of load control and its performance is supported by simulation results.

To investigate the effects of gravity on black string thermodynamics and Hawking radiation in the context of Rastall theory, we analyzed five-dimensional charged black string spacetimes. Our analysis involved deriving the energy-momentum tensor and a modified Einstein's equation for the Rastall theory, from which we obtained the horizons and thermodynamic properties for these black strings. We also examined the influence of a cosmological constant and Rastall parameter on Hawking radiation using the Proca field. Our results show that the Rastall parameter impacts the decay rate of Hawking radiation in various scenarios.

Let $T$ be a weakly contraction mapping on a separable Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Assuming $T$ fulfills certain conditions similar to those found in Toeplitz operators, we establish specifications for its spectral measure $\mathsf{E}$. Furthermore, using the L\"{u}ders theorem, we reveal the spectral type of unitary transformations within the orbit of $T$. This investigation's results are then expanded to cover the non-unitary case. Additionally, we analyze the non-unitary scenario by examining a particular form of Toeplitz operator. Based on these findings, we draw inferences regarding von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. According to a related theorem, weakly convergence in the sense of measure preserves equality when the respective spectral measures are mutually singular. This insight enables us to deduce that the convergence speeds of $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} T^k$ and $T^n$ can be equal, particularly when $T$ corresponds to a Toeplitz operator with an injective spectral measure $\mathsf{E}$.

The data collected by the Gaia space mission, such as the BP/RP spectral energy distributions, can be used to identify metal-poor stars and hydrigen-burning stars in the galaxy. However, these stars have limited brightness and a limited number of observed stars. A machine learning approach was used to improve the selection process of metal-poor stars and take full advantage of the available information in the Gaia database. Initially, a list of the most relevant features was defined, such as the position of the star and its luminosity in the plane. A random forest model was then trained using mock catalog entries and test results showed that it could correctly identify metal-poor stars and hydrogen-burning stars with an error margin of less than 10%. Compared to previous techniques the random forest model and was applied to real data to identify metal-poor stars and hydrogen-burning stars within a specific radius of the sun. A total of 616 metal-poor stars and 894 hydrogen-burning stars were added to the selection which showed a good match with previous studies of metal-poor stars and hydrogen-burning stars. Furthermore, the random forest model was used to improve the selection process of very metal-poor stars and hydrogen-burning stars which could then be applied to real data to identify 161 very metal-poor stars and hydrogen-burning stars within a specific radius of the sun. Finally, the random forest model was used to improve the selection process of metal-poor stars and hydrogen-burning stars

This research uses satellite imagery to study global burn areas and their connection to weather and climate. An algorithm was developed to assemble a comprehensive picture of worldwide burn areas from publicly available satellite data. By analyzing these data over time, we discovered that 2020 was the year with the largest area of burns since the records began in 2003, largely due to increased fires in Australia and Russia. Additionally, our results suggest that climate change could be contributing to an rise in burn areas, particularly in regions with warmer climates, as they are more susceptible to drying and ignition. An statistical model was also built to forecast burn areas worldwide, showing a strong correlation between weather and climate conditions and the intensity of fires.

We've conducted a comprehensive study across 27 languages in an effort to gain more insight into the link between the complexity of words in a language and its properties, such as word order, language type (isolating or inflecting), writing system, and population size. We've also explored the impact of word borrowing and morphological flexibility on complexity, in addition to examining variations in the BERT-Like models' performance across languages of differing complexities. Our research identifies and evaluates several measures of lexical complexity that can serve as a foundation for further research, while discovering inconsistencies in the existing measures of complexity in languages. We've also demonstrated the effectiveness of learning one of these complexity metrics using a language model, specifically a BERT-Like model, which is designed to capture the complexity of words in languages.

Galaxy clusters are crucial for understanding the early universe because they provide valuable information about how gravity works at a small scale. However, since dark matter makes up the majority of clusters, we can't observe it directly and must rely on data from lensed galaxies to study it. The phenomenon of gravitational lensing can either magnify or distort the images of galaxies, depending on the strength of the dark matter field in a particular area. To learn more about the nature of dark matter, we need to accurately measure how it affects these lensed galaxies. We've developed a new method to achieve this, which involves using observations from the Subaru/HSC dataset. The results suggest that if dark matter particles interact with each other, our model predicts a weaker effect on the early universe than if they don't interact at all. When we applied our model to the data, we found that the two models are difficult to tell apart based on the data available. However, our analysis does show that if the models prefer similar magnification effects, a stricter upper limit on their interaction is preferred.

This research focuses on model compression techniques that allow large neural networks to be simplified and reduced in size while maintaining their original performance. Unlike existing methods that require complete access to the entire training dataset, our proposed algorithms can effectively compress models using partial or incomplete datasets, thereby saving significant space and time for large models. Two initial model compression methods were successfully validated on multiple classifications datasets, achieving the same accuracy levels as their full-sized counterparts. Although the compressed models cannot achieve the same accuracy levels on unfamiliar datasets, they demonstrate a consistent trend of outperforming traditional model compression methods. It is also shown that the compressed models can adapt to new tasks and provide effective knowledge transfer. Furthermore, the compressed models can successfully decompose and separate redundant features, reducing the risk of overfitting on familiar datasets.

This work presents the M-ar-K-Rapid independent component analysis (M-ar-K-Rapid ICA) algorithm, offering a new method of estimating weights for Linear Independent Component Analysis based on kernel methods. As kernel-based ICA weight estimation requires solving a small set of kernel matrices, computationally intensive steps like solving a large eigenvector problem or generating a kernel Hessian can be omitted. This research expands upon the previous methods of M-ar-K ICA and Multi-view M-ar-K ICA, enabling faster convergence and greater stability by selecting critical data for kernel-based learning, leveraging stochastic gradient descent to efficiently update kernel matrices. Experimental findings indicate that M-ar-K-Rapid ICA outperforms other benchmark ICA algorithms, while its multi-view extension surpasses other multi-view ICA methods, demonstrating better stability and state-of-the-art performance in sparse and noisy conditions.

Sudden occurrences, such as accidents, break-ins, and emergencies, are emerging topics of interest on social media platforms. Researchers and safety officials are leveraging these discussions to gain insight into incidents in the moment. However, conventional methods for extracting data from social media require specific geo-tagging and timely information, limiting their ability to capture incidents accurately. To address this limitation, our study presents a novel solution that combines geo-located and time-sensitive social media data with machine learning techniques to accurately pinpoint the locations and times of incidents. By comparing traditional methods that rely on search queries with our proposed model's performance, we observed higher average precision and recall rates, particularly off-line averages of 92.07% and 85.43%, respectively. Moreover, our technique significantly reduces online computation requirements by as much as 84%.

We establish results for elliptic operators on R^n that include measures as inputs, specifically when these measures have bounded variation on the surface. Within this framework, under certain conditions, we derive first- and second-order estimates for the operator's action on harmonics. Notably, our findings remain valid for locally integrable functions. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed examination of the case where the operator is an elliptic fractional power.

To address the shortage of rare and valuable resources, such as cobalt, over 300 yttrium-cobalt-boron solid compound structures were examined. Our analysis involved combining computational modeling with the principle of increasing complexity, where we started with established solid compounds and applied evolutionary operations to introduce modifications. Through this process, new cobalt-rich compounds with exceptional potential were discovered, including YCo$_{11}$B$_8$ and YCo$_{15}$B$_5$ in addition to several others. Furthermore, calculations using the phonon calculation tool revealed that some of the discovered compounds may be prone to structural instability. However, when this limitation exists, alternative stable arrangements of the same substances were found. Ultimately, our research highlights the effectiveness and time-saving potential of the computational approach for discovering new solid compounds.

A fundamental issue in online display advertising is creating an optimal bidding strategy that maximizes an advertiser's return on investment while staying within a given budget. Current real-time bidding techniques focus solely on the cost per action metric to decide how much to spend, but this greatly oversimplifies the complex nature of real-world advertising settings. Since the optimal bidding strategy in an ad auction often involves taking multiple gradients of the function relating the chance of success and payment, this paper proposes an innovative bidding strategy called risk-sensitive bidding, which adapts to changing auction conditions by adjusting its strategy based on both the cost per action and a financial stability valve to prevent exceeding the set budget. Using the principles of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning and an adaptive learning strategy called policy mirror descent, this paper presents an algorithm that achieves the best possible balance between the risk of failure and the risk of exceeding the budget while minimizing the overall cost per action. When tested against different scenarios, our findings show that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of the cost per action.

We investigate non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, focusing on quantum transport
properties and the phenomenon of Wigner negativity in higher-order correlation
functions. It emerges that Wigner negativity is a crucial indicator of quantum system
behavior, capable of revealing both quantum and thermal characteristics. We establish
that in non-interacting quantum systems, Nth-order Wigner functions are convex combinations
of separate negative and positive pieces. Furthermore, for interacting non-equilibrium
systems, the statistical operator's negativity and an Nth-order correlation function's
Wigner negativity are both proportional to the quantum Fisher information, thus dependent
on the quantum system's characteristics. We derive exact, closed-form expressions for the
local magnetic susceptibility of a two-component fermionic chain with on-site interactions
and an applied magnetic field. We analyze how the thermal behavior of a non-equilibrium
fermionic system emerges from the guidance that originates in the quantum regime, even
in the absence of electron magnon excitations, which contradicts the Elliott model's
predictions.

Recent research in quantum key distribution data analysis has seen the introduction of a new method to evaluate QKD systems' security, allowing for explicit bound key calculation using random source security analysis. However, conventional random source security models typically assume uniform randomness, unlike many current QKD implementations which use non-uniform random sources. We've modified previous security analysis to accommodate sources with uniformly distributed min-entropy, leveraging the entropy-approximation method to obtain tight security bounds for QKD systems using non-uniform sources. Our approach involves an entanglement-based conversion method using multiple non-uniform random sources to produce uniform randomness, thereby establishing the security of the QKD protocol. We've implemented this security analysis in the SECOQKD tool, enabling practical security evaluation of QKD experiments involving non-uniform random sources.

A curve is deemed a Bertrand curve when a single normal vector field suffices to determine a normal plane containing the curve's tangent vector, implying such curves are characterized by a constant normal curvature variant, specifically a straight line. In this investigation, we identify and differentiate a newly introduced class of non-planar, straight line curves, designated as timelike Bertrand curves within a pseudo Euclidean space, distinguishing between two subcategories: the first comprising curves whose tangent vectors are always null, categorized as null Bertrand curves, and the second consisting of curves whose tangent vectors are always spacelike, termed spacelike Bertrand curves. Additionally, we establish the formulas for calculating the Frenet-Serret frame values for these curves.

The sampling distribution of a Feller diffusion's maximum, evaluated at log-normalization, has been previously determined. This work expands those findings to include the sampling distribution of the diffusion's maximum in multiple, spatially correlated groups of Feller diffusions. It also investigates the statistical combination of independent maxima from Feller diffusions, comparing the performance of traditional methods with a new, specialized approach developed specifically for normally distributed data. Feller diffusions are used as models for various ecological phenomena, such as population abundance and, in particular, the recruitment process in marine species. Therefore, this research has practical implications for estimating and comparing species recruitment patterns.

In this work, we develop a practical approach to analyze the scattering matrix of a quantum emitter connected to a waveguide through an external port, when it interacts with multi-photon states. This systematic method simplifies the diagrammatic calculation of normalised multi-photon states, thereby facilitating a step-by-step derivation of the S-matrix in a lower dimensional space. Consequently, we apply our method effectively to determine the scattering matrix of a quantum emitter coupled to a waveguide, both in single and double photon scenarios, demonstrating a significant reduction in computational complexity, from a 4D to a 1D spatial dimension.

A 2010 analysis revealed that the universe's diffusion rate varies with time according to the equation $g(t) \propto t^{d}$, with the value of the 'index' constant $d$ equalling $1/2$. Notably, this conclusion was drawn using only standard materials and therefore considered absolute. In contrast, we present a different cosmological model where the rate of diffusion is dependent on time, with the equation being $g(t) \propto t^\frac{3(1+a)}{2(1+b)}$. When we consider values of $a=-1$ and $b=-1/2$, we see that our analysis agrees with the completely certain results from the previous study. We also explore the implications of our model on the large-scale interactions between dark energy and rotating particles, only considering the initial interactions to find the rate at which these particles transition from ordinary matter to being part of the dark energy equilibrium mixture to be $f \propto (1+t)^{-\frac{3(1+a)}{2(1+b)}}$. As expected, for the values of $a=-1$ and $b=-1/2$, we see that our model returns the previous study's result. We also see that in our model of negative $a$ and positive $b$, the rate of matter transitioning to dark energy increases exponentially with time, with the rate of matter transitioning to dark energy decreasing exponentially with time for positive $a

This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate Euler's Lemma, a concept that describes a specific property of even integer exponents in relation to Bernoulli numbers. Additionally, this discussion aims to introduce these concepts to upper-level high school students.

Continuous phase modulation (CPM) is a popular modulation scheme used in various wireless applications, including mobile radio, satellite, and cable transmission. One of the main advantages of CPM is its ability to offer a balance between bandwidth and delay, although this delay can be significantly impacted by the method of differential detection used. In fact, the majority of CPM demodulators utilize a single differential circuit, which can lead to substantial increase in the signal processing delay. This delay worsens with increasing values of the modulation index, making it essential to find an alternative method of detection that can reduce the signal processing delay without compromising bandwidth. In this paper, we investigate non-coherent detection using a single differential circuit and analyze its phase processing delay. Additionally, we examine a technique in which a bandpass filter is employed to mitigate the phenomenon of the "doubler effect," which is responsible for the excessive delay. However, these methods are limited in their effectiveness, with the double differential circuit resulting in a signal processing delay that is only 5.29 times lesser than the standard double method. In contrast, we present an innovative solution where a single "early" sampler is utilized in conjunction with a "late" energy detector to obtain performance comparable to the standard double differential circuit. Notably, this novel approach eliminates the double differential circuit and thereby reduces the signal processing delay to a minimum of 5.29 times. Furthermore, we explore an alternative method where a "late" sampler is employed in conjunction with

Robotic reward learning often relies on a tedious and costly approach, as it involves
manually adjusting variables and measuring outcomes to optimize its performance.
This study aims to reduce reward bias and streamline the reward learning process by
grouping influential parameters into logical categories based on visual representations.
These parameter clusters can then be efficiently ranked in terms of their overall impact,
saving researchers significant amounts of time and resources.
Real-world experiments involving a sophisticated surgical robot have demonstrated the
benefits of this method, as it consistently produced superior results compared to a randomly
selected reward, reduced the time and effort required for manual adjustment, and yielded
outcomes that aligned with surgeon expectations.

We've determined the nucleon configuration functions in the noncommutative space-time with a static electric field. From these functions, the quasiprobability distribution of finding a quark and an antiquark inside a nucleon is constructed. Additionally, the expected distribution in a proton and a neutron is compared.

In typical topological systems, the edge entropy of these models remains stable and peaceful at finite temperature, exhibiting a gradual decrease from the interior value, denoted as the topological edge, which shields the bulk from thermal influence. Contrary to this conventional understanding, several research studies have recently reported that certain materials exhibiting topological properties due to frustration exhibit opposing behavior at room temperature, characterized by a gapped bulk but an entropically dominant topologically degenerate edge. Our research centers on two simplified versions of the Kitaev chain: the ring and boundary models. Using a calculative approach, we demonstrate that the boundary model, plagued by frustration, features high topological edge entropy that far exceeds the bulk value, in contrast to its ring counterpart. Furthermore, the effects of time-varying drivences on the system are investigated, revealing the emergence of topologically degenerate states at resonance frequencies. Introducing a new quantum computing metric, the "topological volume," we can measure the extent of topological edge entropy in circular models. Our research enables us to forecast that the topological effect will persist in related boundary models. Additionally, the effects of minor imperfections on the topological edge are studied.

We investigate how orthogonal matrix ensembles with a disordered, randomly fluctuating potential influence the eigenvalue distribution of their associated Hamiltonian. The analyses provided apply whether the potential is drawn from a narrow distribution with weak support or a more complex, uniformly distributed pattern. The calculations rely on the optical model, which assumes that the matrices' diagonal elements contribute negligible influence. Based on this, we derive an approximation formula for the eigenvalue distribution, which accurately replicates the full spectral shift function when the rank of the random potential is 1. For larger-rank potentials, we demonstrate that the optical model's predictions remain valid and yield a divisible form of the spectral shift function that better aligns with numerical simulations than a previous, lower-rank approximation formula.

Recent years have seen remarkable breakthroughs in conversation understanding through large pre-trained models such as BERT and its variants. Nonetheless, conventional pre-training methods utilizing masked language prediction and next-sentence prediction overlook the underlying semantics of conversations, despite their effectiveness in building end-to-end conversation systems. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel pre-training strategy that incorporates a context-based semantic analysis, along with a further refinement of the BERT framework. By leveraging a high-performance context matcher to enhance conversation comprehension, we find our proposed method substantially boosts performance in task-specific fine-tuning, particularly for critical conversation understanding tasks like recognizing conversation topics, tracking entities, and predicting conversation lengths.

Machine learning algorithms have always struggled to explain their predictions and workings to humans. In an attempt to standardize interpretability evaluations, researchers proposed a new approach that focuses on how well these explanations help humans understand the learning system. They developed a comprehensive framework consisting of three key elements: the ability of an algorithm to adjust its explanation based on the learning system's performance, the ability to pinpoint the factors most relevant to that performance, and the ability to accurately predict human questions and adapt to them. In the process of assessing this new approach, the researchers tested it against existing measures of interpretability and found that it offered unique insights. They also applied their framework to various machine learning models across different data types and discovered some interesting patterns, which could potentially lead to improved algorithm design.

Anomaly detection without data ID remains a stubborn problem in edge computing environments. The conventional techniques, relying on cloud-managed databases, struggle to process AI algorithms at the edge due to limited resources. A promising approach is to develop compact, self-sustaining anomaly detectors using unsupervised isolated anomaly detection. However, these methods typically require a significant number of clean anomalies to set an optimal threshold. Without a reliable anomaly inventory, the anomaly detection accuracy suffers from improper threshold settings. To address this issue, we introduce TiWS-iForest, an isolation tree-based method optimized for tiny, weakly-guided scenarios, including sensor data analysis without labeling. TiWS-iForest achieves this with smaller tree sizes, lower memory requirements, and improved stability by integrating data normalization, limited-depth trees, and weighted scoring. In comparison to iForest, TiWS-iForest demonstrates a 52x reduction in tree size, an 11x boost in detection frequency, an 8x enhancement in precision, and an 6x increase in recall, all while showcasing stability even without a clear lead in clean anomalies.

A novel approach that combines a non-stationary Poisson process with a temporal transformation is presented for analyzing extreme events within a Bayesian framework. Given the inability to model extreme values using traditional, parametric models due to their rare occurrence, Poisson process autoregressives have been proposed as an alternative semi-parametric model. However, one of the limitations of this approach is that it requires time series data with a relatively low level of noise. To overcome this limitation, a new method involves applying a transformation to the time scale to increase the variability of the data. A full Bayesian analysis is developed for this multi-scale representation, with the model parameters determined through combination with an underlying distribution. Focusing on the typical case of stationary, identically distributed, and independent extreme values, a Bayesian analysis is presented for estimating the parameters of this distribution. A simulation study demonstrates the feasibility of this method under realistic conditions mimicking a real-world analysis of sea level rise data.

The formula for calculating the average cross section in a given area has been established, as well as the conditions required for the cross section to achieve a stationary value.  A method for identifying the optimal area where the cross section reaches its stationary value has been developed, relying on the sign of the second derivative of the cross section in that area.  If the second derivative is positive, this area represents a minimum; with a negative derivative, it's a maximum.  A graphical representation of the process was also provided, illustrating how to determine which area reaches a stationary value.

Common sense knowledge can be represented in two forms - knowledge stored in memory and knowledge used in problem-solving. To compare and study this knowledge, we've created a dataset containing 50,000 real-world examples of everyday objects, actions, and emotions, along with their associated attributes. This dataset is based on a large online text collection and defines the relationships between objects, actions, and emotions. To test the effectiveness of learning this knowledge, we've used compressive neural network models and symbolic reasoning techniques to analyze the dataset. Our results show that symbolic reasoning is effective in understanding its components, while neural networks show improvement in understanding action-knowledge and emotion-knowledge due to their hierarchical structure. This knowledge dataset is available online for research purposes.

We present a groundbreaking 70 $\mu$m map of the Milky Way's inner regions following the removal of extraneous information from the PLANCK/Homi survey. To generate the cleaned map, we employed a data processing pipeline that leveraged spectral information, spatial correlations, and cross-referencing of satellite observations. The resulting clean 70 $\mu$m map, named Hi-GAL $70$, is comprised of 1200 tiles and forms the cornerstone of the Hi-GAL atlas, an indispensable piece of the EMPIRE survey repertoire. The Hi-GAL $70$ map serves as input for the various Hi-GAL teams working on source extraction, component analysis, and physical modeling as part of the EMPIRE survey initiative.

The two brightest globular clusters in the Milky Way, NGC 2808 and NGC 4590, present exceptional cases due to their unusual metal abundance distributions and extremely high stellar mass-to-light ratios. By using the high-resolution optical spectrum of seven bright stars from NGC 2808 measured with the HARPS-NOVAS instrument, we derived precise metal abundances and stellar surface gravities. The resulting data clearly demonstrate a bimodal metal distribution in NGC 2808 with means of -0.84 and -0.18 and a significant gap in between. This finding reinforces previous findings and supports the hypothesis of a metal abundance disparity within this cluster. Furthermore, our new data reduce the uncertainty in estimating the metal abundance of individual stars to a range of 0.04-0.13 dex, depending on the star's signal-to-noise ratio.

A crucial aspect of any binding process is the duration of the initial wait period, known as the phasic stage. For the case of a moving particle encountering a fixed opening in a one-dimensional lane with limited space, we develop an approximate expression for the probability distribution of this wait period, deriving it through a method based on the principle of minimum entropy. Notably, this expression for the distribution of initial wait periods matches the numerical results extremely well. Moreover, it allows for an easy calculation of the average duration. Additionally, it can also be utilized to establish the influence of temperature and bond strength, as well as the effects of varying binding parameters, all of which are crucial considerations for the design of biosensors. What's more, this method can be directly applied to other types of binding processes, offering a versatile approach in the field of biophysical chemistry.

Quantum physics challenges traditional notions of reality, reality's perception, and the framework for making inferences. To address these complexities, this paper draws on a powerful theorem initially described by Russell and then applied in a broad context by Hoyle and Russell. This theorem serves as the foundation for an innovative proof of quantum mechanics' coherence, highlighting how quantum phenomena solidify the underlying inference model. Specifically, this paper explores two compelling instances: first, it examines entanglement-based nonlocality through the example of Bell's experiment; second, it delves into the inherent uncertainty principle illustrated by the specific case of quantum interference. The findings presented unify two apparently contradictory perspectives on quantum phenomena, reconciling the principles of reality maintenance and inductive inference with the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

The QCD Equation of State (EoS) defines the relationship between energy density and pressure within a system of quarks and gluons. Significant to the universe's early stages, this relationship plays a rising role in studying quantum matter under extreme conditions, such as high temperatures and zero or low densities. Recent advances in multi-messenger astrophysics and gravitational wave detection have also heightened the importance of EoS in studying relativistic quantum systems. While various novel EoS methods have been developed, their reliability for specific applications remains an active area of debate. In particular, there is ongoing research into whether these approaches accurately capture the EoS's distinct phases, particularly the critical point and critical temperature, and whether they're applicable at very low and high densities. To address these concerns, this work focuses on a new approach - the state function of tiny systems - representing a separate aspect of QCD's phase diagram and less susceptible to these issues. Introducing a corresponding observable, this work demonstrates its potential for guiding the development of conventional EoS and identifying essential characteristics of QCD's phase diagram, particularly its critical properties. As such, this observable offers a compromise for simplifying complex phase diagram investigations while still providing valuable insights into QCD's intricate physics.

The Steenrod algebra's graded coalgebra $A_{\mathbb{F}_2}$, parameterized by non-negative integers $n$, contains specific elements $s_i$ where $1\leq i\leq n$. These elements, part of a fundamental generator set in the $n^{th}$ coalgebra level, interact directly with the $i^{th}$ coordinate of any element within that generator set's associated vector space. As a result, when working through a product operation in $A_{\mathbb{F}_2}$, the effect of other generator set elements on the $i^{th}$ coordinate becomes apparent, due to the direct interaction mentioned. Consequently, the interplay between generator set elements, particularly in how they multiply together, becomes significant in understanding the topology defined by the spectral sequence derived from Graded Adem Relations. This realization, crucial in its own right, is only more important when the topology is applied in analyzing cohomology rings of classifying spaces for families, particularly in the ignoring or non-ignoring of those critical coalgebra elements $s_i$.

Astronomers observe the universe primarily through visible and ultraviolet light captured by space-based telescopes such as the Hubble Space Telescope. However, this mission' ultraviolet capability is currently limited due to the presence of interstellar and extragalactic light which overpowers and distorts the light signals from celestial objects. To rectify this issue, we developed an innovative approach - the Lyman filter model, a data processing technique that can be used on future space-based telescopes, enabling us to accurately decode the original light signals from stars and other celestial objects and reconstruct their natural spectra. Our Lyman filter model is highly effective, offering several key benefits including minimizing the impact of Lyman-alpha foreground emission and recovering the lost ultraviolet light signals from stars. Additionally, this model can correctly apply the white noise from the original light signals and accurately estimate its magnitude, while also identifying and distorting electromagnetic noise and accurately cutting off the distorted signal at its point of termination. As a result, this model offers a significant breakthrough in enabling accurate light capture from celestial objects in the Lyman ultraviolet range and the broader astronomy community, with far-reaching implications for various scientific research activities.

A key constraint of spectral filtering methods for graph signal processing is the requirement for access to node degree information, which can be difficult to obtain in large-scale networks.  To overcome this limitation, this research proposes a new class of decentralized controllers that leverages graph filters to regulate node activities in large networks without needing degree information.  By design, these controllers disperses autonomy evenly among nodes, resulting in stable behavior and consistent performance.  We show that these controllers have consistent effects on network dynamics when applied to various types of compatible networks and provide an example of how these controllers can be used to improve the stability of a multi-node oscillator system.

This paper outlines a novel technique for automatically categorizing images based on the dynamic facial expressions present within them. A computationally efficient algorithm was developed that accurately detects and normalizes both individual and grouped images, followed by a support vector machine classification of the normalized images. A comprehensive dataset consisting of 1,501 image files, featuring diverse dynamic facial expressions, was utilized to test and validate the proposed method against other established image classification techniques. Notably, our approach achieved a significantly higher accuracy rate of 90.25% on the test dataset, compared to the 83.76% achieved by the next highest method.
