The Transformer model's innovative yet intricate architecture has sparked interest among researchers who are working to uncover its capabilities and underlying behaviors. This paper summarizes the model's key advancements and reviews the literature on topics such as enhanced transformers, multi-modal processing, and the model's applications, in order to provide a comprehensive overview of its current state. The discussion also highlights potential challenges and areas of future research, including handling sequence lengths and model complexities, that could leverage the model's strengths.

The purpose of this paper is to create a forecast tool for mortality that utilizes factor models and accounts for the time-dependent characteristics of factor loadings in a model's structural equation framework. We explore different approaches for updating a initial model's factor loadings on an ongoing basis, incorporating changes into a separate sub-model. Our various strategies for incorporating changes into factor loadings are evaluated in the context of a large dataset on U.S. life insurance data. The results indicate that a factor model with time-variant factor loadings exhibits fewer problems than a time-constant model, particularly when reconstructing a previously estimated model from scratch. When comparing different methods for updating factor loadings, we find that a strategy based on separate sub-models for each period performs better than one that uses pooled data for all periods, while a strategy that uses regression on changes has the least predictive power. Overall, the need for updating a model's factor loadings depends on how factors change over time, and efficient results can be achieved by analyzing multiple periods separately if the relationship between factors and time is non-essential.

Researchers have recently demonstrated the potential of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) in auto-selecting architectures for tasks such as image classification and object detection. However, current top-tier NAS models exhibit significantly slower training speeds than traditional randomly-generated models only because they incorporate a set of hand-designed base architectures. This problem persists due to the training data's interference, which impairs the training of NAS models on previously solved tasks. In an attempt to resolve this issue, we have developed an innovative method to finely tune randomly-generated architectures without disrupting their parameterization. Moreover, we have developed another technique that eliminates interference and allows NAS models to learn from previously trained tasks. In experiments, we have observed significant performance enhancements, with combined achievements of up to 8.0% on the CIFAR-10 dataset and up to 4.3% on the ImageNet dataset. Our achievements were independently validated using two NAS methods and verified against randomly-generated models.

Time series data analysis often requires attribute-based examination, 
which involves exploring and manipulating time series data based on specific attributes.
The THEFT package for R provides a set of functions designed to accommodate 
time series data examination with both intrinsic and extrinsic attributes.
This package includes features for attribute management, data quality control, 
querying data, splitting and combining datasets, and duplicating existing time series.
Various supporting tools like attribute encoding, duplication, and querying are also available, 
along with functions for data visualization through both classic and interactive methods 
and a dashboard for interactive attribute-based time series analysis.
This package offers a unified solution for all aspects of attribute-based time series analysis.

This research focuses on the set EdGC, comprising all edges in the boundary of a geodesically complete CAT(0) space. We've established that EdGC shares certain characteristics with the set of conical ends, identified an intrinsic 1-parameter group moduli associated with elements of EdGC, demonstrated a non-trivial action of SL_2(Z) on EdGC under specific conditions, and also proved that EdGC is a stable subset within the space of all rigid geodesic spaces. Furthermore, our work includes an examination of rigid isometry groups within the context of geodesically complete, proper, and bornological spaces.

Translator evaluation is an essential component of machine translation assessment,–a process traditionally relied upon by the machine learning industry. Human translator evaluations are crucial, yet the method is limited in its capacity to capture individual translators' level of reliability. This study outlines a statistical technique for evaluating the dependability of human translators, utilizing a subset of available data. By classifying multiple translator evaluations as accurate or inaccurate, and utilizing a translator's overall evaluation set as sample data to calculate their dependability score, we obtain a reliable measure. Furthermore, this method can also provide a confidence interval for dependability scores, using Bayesian statistics. This study further explores the challenges of evaluating machine translation, discussing validation set selection, translator pool size, and performance evaluation.

We derive three fundamental theorems governing energy absorption by nonradiative and radiative defects in disordered, nonordered, and ordered systems. These formulas express the deflection of classical and quantum flow through nonradiative and radiative defects in disordered, nonordered, and ordered systems in terms of energy absorption. Similar to eigenchannel concepts for scattering intensity, each theorem attributes energy absorption to a defect alone when it's averaged over all incident wave functions, and this average value is unaffected by the wave function's specific form. We confirm these concepts through numerical examples based on the Anderson and Coulomb models.

We've taken the benchmark CUB bird dataset and removed the effects of its pre-training on a massive dataset of 120 million images by decoupling its deep network from the vast dataset it was trained on. This allowed us to isolate how much improvement came from learning a specific class's characteristics rather than just generalizing to the data it was trained on. To achieve this, we first converted the network's weights to an unlearned basis, and then truncated the network to various sizes of 20 to 119, repeating this process hundreds of times. Our findings show that as we go from the unlearned basis to the size of 49, the performance of the trimmed network surpasses that of the massive pre-trained network, with the size of 49 being the optimal point. Moreover, although retraining the trimmed network to convergence leads to slightly better results, the difference is extremely small. This means that rather than needing a massive dataset and a massive network, we could achieve similar results with a relatively small dataset and a humble amount of computing resources. This also supports the idea that rather than needing to continue training a network to perfection, we could achieve similar results with a much simpler network.

This research suggests a method for individuals to mitigate the unpleasant surprise of a disappointing lottery win by analyzing the potential outcome. By applying the principles of regression quantiles, we develop a unique prediction model. Our prediction model is highly versatile and suitable for any type of lottery. Additionally, we create an index that measures the performance of different lotteries and assesses their potential value to participants. Our analysis, based on data from the National Survey of Family Growth, offers a unique perspective on the relationship between the odds of a lottery and the degree of disappointment experienced by the winner. Our findings indicate that, on average, a double-zero bet is the least undesirable option among all the bets offered by casinos.

This work is focused on calculating the six-loop contributory term of the unusual dimension of the $\phi^Q$ operator in the $O(N)$-symmetric phi^Q model. Calculations involve a special type of integral that can accommodate operators of various dimensions. These integrals can be broken down into simpler 'parallel' integrals with the same beta functions as in the $O(N)$-symmetric phi^4 model. Additionally, some new five-loop integrals are also developed for operators of lower dimensionality. Using this method, we've determined the anomalous dimension at the one-loop order for all $O(N)$-symmetric operators to the six-loop order. These calculations were particularly straightforward for operators involving dimensions of one, thanks to the availability of a simplified integral representation. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that while some six-loop orders match those of the phi^4 model, others do so only in the limit of large Q. Additionally, we've derived some relationships between the coefficients of the effective action in the phi^4 model and those of the phi^6 operator. Finally, we've also shown how the unusual dimension contributes to the conformal fixed point in the phi^6 operator.

To study the behavior of valleys in two-dimensional materials, we need to look at different types of interactions between electrons and phonons. We've developed a framework to analyze these interactions based on the material's properties and symmetry. This way, we can compare different calculations of valley excitations in materials like graphene and single-layer TMDs to understand their relationships. We find that a particular form of interaction that involves both mid-gap and resonant phonons can lead to a connection between these excitations, which isn't captured by other methods. This new approach helps us predict the behavior of valley physics in low-temperature single-layer MoS2 crystals.

We successfully applied our adapted multi-stage learning strategy, developed for
the NeurIPS 2021 VisAD Challenge, to the NeurIPS 2022 VisAD Challenge. The
challenge this year involved domain adaptation on atmospheric imagery. Our
approach to the problem involved four stages of deep learning-based image
processing, starting with a coarse domain normalization task, followed by
atmospheric image denoising, and then two classification tasks aimed at
identifying the type of cloud and its spatial distribution across the image. We
relied on a comprehensive set of experimental evaluations to refine our method,
which ultimately achieved exceptional results across all tasks in the official
evaluations. Our method's effectiveness was further validated by a close
examination of its components. We are pleased to announce that our technique
earned top honors in all three primary evaluations: overall performance, method
simplicity, and computational efficiency.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data down to lower dimensions, particularly in the field of visualization. Its core principle of preserving local similarities in a nonlinear manner has minimal application beyond 3D data structures, as it relies on Euclidean distances in lower dimensions. In cases involving spherical data structures such as protein structures where traditional t-SNE applications fail, alternative distance metrics like geodesic distance are necessary. This research presents an extension of classical t-SNE to spherical surfaces, preserving local similarities while accurately modeling spherical data structures through an enhanced nearest neighbor search that leverages spherical geometry. This modified t-SNE variant, referred to as VMF-SNE, has been implemented within the Coot molecular visualization software. Moreover, a thorough benchmarking framework is provided to benchmark and evaluate novel dimensionality reduction methods performing optimizations on protein structures.

We utilize the powerful tool of diagrammatic Monte Carlo in the system with a Fermi polaron to significantly enhance fermion-particle correlations that the conventional Eulerian scaling is based on. This advancement enables us to accurately compute the ground state energy of the system and the activation energy associated with the Eulerian scaling, which significantly differs from previous results where an infinite scaling limit was applied. This new finding sheds light on the underlying reasons for the Eulerian scaling's failure and points out that the Eulerian scaling fails to adequately represent fermion-particle correlations, which are crucial in the polaron system. Meanwhile, the activation energy associated with the Eulerian scaling in two dimensions exhibits a logarithmic increase with the U / k inter-particle coupling, and this logarithmic increase suggests that the Eulerian scaling fails by an amount of the order of ( U / k ) ^{-2}.

Recent advancements in quantum processing have led to a shift in interest from traditional analog computing methods to hybrid digital-analog approaches, particularly in simulating complex physical systems. Digital-analog hybrids offer a significant advantage by allowing for more efficient simulation of fermionic and bosonic systems, given that analog circuits are particularly beneficial for managing large numbers of fermions. By leveraging the strength of analog circuits in simulating fermionic systems and the efficiency of digital circuits in quantum information management, a new hybrid digital-analog protocol can outperform both pure digital and pure analog protocols in certain applications.

Graph characteristics are a collection of polynomial-based attributes that illustrate various numerical facets of a given graph. As an example, the Eulerian polynomial captures the count of a graph's Eulerian vertices, while the matching polynomial tracks the number of maximal independent sets within a given graph. In this investigation, we examine a group of graph invariants derived from the intersection of two characteristic polynomials, initially identified by Rowlinson and, later independently, by Bogdanowicz and Bollobás in relation to the independent dominating set problem. We reveal a precise, explicit formula for the coefficients in the expansion of the difference of these two polynomials, a query that had previously been posed by Bogdanowicz and Bollobás in an unsolved state. Our innovative approach combines a transformation bounded by a 2k+3 supervertex star graph, a recursive definition, and a clean attribution, alongside the use of the Sun-Zhang theorem, in resolving this question. Additionally, we derive implicit descriptions for the graphs in which the absolute value of the coefficient of the i'th term in the expansion of the difference of the independent set and dominating set polynomials is greater than that of all other terms, a concept which we have referred to as 'extremophilic graphs'.

We establish a detailed description of a refined version of the Hitchin link, specifically in the hyperbolicization of the Veech curve associated with the 9-gon. This curved surface was initially studied by Gromadka and Zgagowski, who proved that it features an extended anosov structure with a unique saddle node surface. Our work involves demonstrating that the volume of the corresponding core of the residual flow is finite and developing a precise analytic expression for it, analogous to previous results obtained by the second author for a generic curved surface in a related paper.

This investigative study delves into the consequences of remote work on the effectiveness of Scrum projects through a qualitative, quantitative investigation. First, a literature review assesses the relevance of working remotely in the context of Agile management. Subsequently, a quantitative study based on 416 responses from software professionals was conducted to analyze the impact of remote work on Scrum project outcomes. The data were collected via an online survey focusing on cross-functional teams working with Scrum framework in Germany and the United States. The responses were analyzed in relation to working remotely and their impact on project success, as well as the role of collaborative activities such as coding reviews and sprints. The data were tested for multivariate normality and several variables were adjusted accordingly. A series of hierarchical multiple linear regression models were analyzed with specified criteria, including adjustment of collinear variables, selection of relevant variables, and evaluation of residual assumptions. The results indicate that working remotely can compromise the traditional concepts of cross-functional teams and co-located work, although it can facilitate access to a broader and more international pool of talent. A pre-coded email survey of 67 software professionals was also conducted to provide qualitative insights into the implementation of Scrum in distributed teams, resulting in the identification of best practices through a qualitative analysis. The results of this study can aid software managers in implementing Scrum methodologies in remote work settings, alongside offering suggestions for practicing remote work and cross-functional collaboration.

The study of the Gau-Wu value for arrowhead matrices of any size is a previously unexplored area of research. This investigation focuses on determining one-parameter matrices of the arrowhead form for 4x4 matrices and calculates their Gau-Wu values. As an extension of the research, Gau-Wu values are verified for special cases of these matrices, specifically when the lower left 2x2 corner consists of a zero entry.

The elliptical movement of particles, such as protons, antiprotons, charged pions, and kaons, created in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC's 5.02 TeV, has been measured and compared to similar events involving beauty hadrons. These beauty hadrons were detected by combining ALICE with data from LHCb, resulting in a study with a broader range of hadrons and more statistics collected near the centre of the collision. These findings show a significant difference between particles produced directly from beauty hadrons and those produced independently. Indications are that the separation of particles, caused by the collision's stress, is greater for particles produced together from beauty hadrons than for individual particles. A significant variation in the elliptical movement of particles, especially in their momentum ranges, supports current theoretical models of how particles move under stress upon collision. These models will be further studied and developed with the accumulated data.

New concepts in equivariant homotopy theory are driving the development of sophisticated studies in advanced mathematical fields such as topological, periodic, and algebraic topology, inspiring contributions to the study of exotic braids and shedding light on key questions regarding the steady homotopy theory of important mathematical objects, particularly infinite loop spaces and chromatic abelian categories, leading to the establishment of critical outcomes in the study of stable and univalent homotopy theory; this work introduces the chromatic alpha structures, establishing their stability and splitting them univately, while efficiently calculating their univalent counterparts, paving the way for further advancements in the field of steady homotopy theory.

The global Drew (GDoF) of interference networks with $K$ transmitters and $K$ receivers is a measure of the telegraphy GDoF for a network with $K$ independent source messages, where each node regulates its transmission power to either 0 or 1 (binary power control) or optimally adjusts its transmission power based on message indices (optimal power control). Previous research has shown that the difference in GDoF between optimal and binary power control in a $K$ transmitter and receiver network is at most $\sqrt{K}$ and at least $\sqrt{K}/2$, which indicates the extremal GDoF benefit of optimal power control is bounded within a range of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This research shows the benefit of optimal power control over binary power control in networks with $K$ transmitters and receivers is strictly greater than $\sqrt{K}$ and less than $\sqrt{K}\cdot K$, which indicates the extremal GDoF benefit of optimal power control is bounded within a range of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. When combined with previous research, it is known that the benefit of optimal power control over binary power control in networks with $K$ transmitters and receivers is at most $K$ and at least $\sqrt{K}$, which indicates the benefit of optimal power control is bounded within a range of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This research shows the benefit of optimal power control over binary power

In the context of automated auditing, our goal is to identify misclassified activities as outliers. To achieve this, we develop a cutting-edge adaptive system that facilitates real-time classification across multiple scenarios. By integrating multiple models in real-time, the classifier adjusts its strategy accordingly to ensure accuracy. To further enhance outcome reliability, we employ two techniques: formal concept analysis to validate the decision outcome and Dempster-Shafer theory to assess uncertainty levels. A high-level overview of the proposed classification method is provided in the paper, which is accompanied by a detailed simulation study showcasing its effectiveness and performance evaluation.

This study examines two techniques for creating point patterns in a specific area: 
the Strauss model. This particular model is of particular interest in the statistics field 
due to the conditions under which it forms a proper distribution. The techniques 
under evaluation produce realistic patterns, and their efficacy is assessed through 
visual and numerical assessments. The method demonstrating better results utilizes 
the process of stitching to create these patterns. As a result of this method's success, 
we apply it in two distinct contexts: the creation of realistic, high-density point 
patterns and the generation of confidence intervals for the parameter beta used 
in the Strauss model.

In the context of string theory, quantum gravity, and the generalized uncertainty principle, the modified relativistic principle has previously been explored from a semi-classical perspective, leading to a modified Schwarzschild metric. This paper builds upon those findings by determining the potential impact of the generalized uncertainty principle on symmetry alterations, specifically Galilean and Lorentz, through a systematic analysis. By comparing the modified gravitational force to the generalized uncertainty force, the modified Schwarzschild potential is derived, and its implications on Galilean symmetry are discussed. Furthermore, the potential impact on Lorentz symmetry is explored through a modified Doppler effect.

In timetabling, the primary goal is to efficiently allocate time slots for concurrently optimized scheduling of students and teachers. We've developed Multitasking Teacher-Student Timetabling (MTST), a new framework for solving large timetabling problems by simultaneously optimizing the schedules of both students and teachers. MTST uses teacher-student pairs, allowing the direct allocation of time slots while adhering to constraints through the integration of an existing algorithm with added optimizations. We've also developed two variants of the MTST solution, which initially allocates time slots for teachers and then students, or begins with student time slots and adjusts teacher schedules, both utilizing teacher-student pair constraints to enhance solution quality. We've tested our approach on 28 datasets from the Timetabling Competition and compared it favorably with the current best solution, achieving a 20.36% improvement in overall measures and 16.30% improvement in individual measures.

A simplified model for a one-legged hopping robot has been developed, accounting for how it/deformable ground interact. An initial simulation revealed that the ground's yield point has a significant impact on the robot's movement, suggesting that altering the ground's stiffness could enhance its performance. Further models were created to explore this idea: a "spring-ground" model with extra flexibility and a "ground-slip model" simulating increased sliding friction. Simulation results indicated that modifying the leg's tip and adding a grip texture could significantly improve the robot's hopping efficiency. Experimenting with these designs using a one-legged robot made of 3D-printed components successfully demonstrated its advantages.

In the rapidly expanding landscape of IoT systems, the need for swift and seamless software updates is becoming increasingly vital, especially as these updates frequently coincide with security-enhancing patches. The convergence of IoT devices and the rise of the shared mesh network is significantly affecting wireless communications, causing conventional wireless capacity models to fall short. Consequently, the efficiency of software updates within mesh networks has been poorly understood, mainly due to the lack of unified evaluation protocols and comprehensive, wide-scale evaluation methodologies. To bridge this knowledge gap, we have carried out an extensive, large-scale measurement of mesh network deployments, assessing their characteristics and the efficacy of firmware updates across different devices, and making all related data available for further research through an open-access platform. Our detailed analysis highlights the considerable time-consuming nature of software upgrades, primarily attributed to prolonged mesh backhaul delays, and reveals that the choice of mesh network devices, network load, and the number of associated devices substantially influence update times, largely in accordance with previously proposed models. Notably, however, the choice of frequency for firmware updates, devices' age, and the number of previous updates, all play a significant role in determining total upgrade time, and tend to contradict the proposed models.

We analyze the eigenstate overlap of many-body localized and delocalized systems using the block multi-fractal analysis of the eigenstate wavefunctions. The eigenstate overlap is utilized as a phase-space dynamical indicator that experiences a strong change in the non-thermal phase. Our investigation shows that the multi-fractal spectrum of the overlap's scaling function is distinct for localized and delocalized systems, has a low-scaled limit of one in the former case, and exhibits a low-scaled low-energy behavior of the latter case that aligns with known results. Additionally, the multi-fractal properties of many-body localized systems are found to have a minimal impact on their dynamics.

This study addresses a complex multi-objective search problem, where an agent aims to locate several targets on a grid in the minimum time possible, while adhering to a query limit. Each query yields information about the agent's current location relative to the targets, and can positively identify a target with a certain probability. Although the targets' locations are fully observable through queries, they can only be confirmed after further queries, as per the conditions specified in Pachocki and Strazditzis' work. A novel query strategy, based on a grid-based exploration approach, is introduced to maximize the probability of finding and identifying all targets within the designated query limit. A novel query strategy is presented which asymptotically achieves a confirmation probability of at least 1/2, along with bounds on the expected number of queries required to confirm multiple targets.

Theoretical examinations of quantum machine learning models have thus far focused largely on their performance against randomly generated input samples. In contrast, this work investigates how these models respond to purposefully constructed instances of greater complexity. To this end, we have developed two sets of such instances: (i) attacks designed to expose the limitations of quantum support vector machine classifiers; and (ii) disturbances intended to assess the robustness of quantum k-nearest neighbors classifiers on both binary and multi-class tasks. In the evaluation of these instances within experimental contexts, our findings indicate that in accordance with their anticipated functionality, they prove particularly effective against the more fragile quantum models while being largely ineffectual against their more robust quantum counterparts.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues of nearly spherical areas, imposing a Hardy inequality, and we investigate how these eigenvalues change in relation to variations in region shape. In specific cases, such as regions bounded by concentric spheres with constant curvature, solutions become particularly straightforward. We also discuss an application involving a shape optimization problem in electrostatically shielding a charge.

Nonconformity exposure is a serious issue that can severely impact trust in a blockchain network, and to prevent this, a new method has been developed. It enables blockchain operators to ensure that individual transaction blocks adhere to a specified format. Our approach leverages the concepts of prefix, infix, and postfix alignments to verify compliance with a given template in O(n) time, independent of the template's structure. It's particularly beneficial, exhibiting an optimal linear time complexity, regardless of the size or complexity of the template. Additionally, this method allows for the evaluation of both fixed and variable-length patterns. Furthermore, this method aligns with existing compliance verification methods that utilize fixed-size patterns and demonstrates compatibility with them.

This research explores the application of a specific type of neural network, called convolutional neural networks (CNNs), in modeling signal propagation within complex mobile networks. The study begins by reviewing conventional approaches to this task and highlights their limitations. The researchers then introduce a novel CNN-based model that effectively captures all key factors influencing signal strength. The novel CNN model outperforms existing methods in accuracy, while offering the significant advantage of not requiring manual data analysis or network planning software. The analysts also examine the model's ability to predict unknown output and find that it can reliably generalize to untested scenarios. The paper concludes with suggestions for further investigation into this type of CNN-based modeling approach.

This research presents a formal validation of the Official semantics for temporal planning problems and their solutions, providing a comprehensive foundation for assessing and comparing different high-level temporal planning algorithms. We formally define the problem status with regards to hierarchy and controllability, and prove that using a certain decision procedure can confidently conclude the termination or intractability of planning tasks. These findings are built upon a previously established study by Byrd and Smith (2014), and are subsequently extended to encompass multi-step (serial) and concurrent (parallel) planning strategies. We demonstrate the practical applicability of our approach to validate planning tasks within the IPBP architecture.

Power grid models are employed to decide whether new infrastructure, such as transmission lines, should be built to handle projected energy demands and production. The decision analysis methods involve several models including optimal network expansion models and linear models with congestion congestion-concerning constraints, which we will refer to as CC models. This study assesses the performance of these models in predicting energy flows on the network and identifies their strengths and limitations in guiding investment decisions. Our investigation utilizes a real-world power network instance with various loads and generating sources, and it reveals that both models frequently fail to adhere to physical network principles, leading to concerns about relying solely on these models for decision-making purposes.

In the past few years, there has been a growing interest in systems related to the Vlasov-Poisson model, which describes the motion of ionized gases under their own electric and magnetic forces. These systems, however, have received limited research particularly regarding their behavior when contained within a bounded area. This study establishes the results of Vlasov-Vlasov-Poisson and Vlasov-Landau systems within enclosed spaces, including the crucial outcome that these systems have a well-defined, global, and unique solution given specific initial conditions. This achievement builds upon previous research on these models when they are assumed to be in a state of neutral stability. Notably, the proof of the system's well-defined nature, in this case, involves a far more intricate process due to the absence of a dissipative mechanism, which is present in systems modeling systems with a single particle distribution. Even so, the method employed in this study, which relies on a combination of energy and kinetic estimates, has the potential to be widely applicable in similar models and systems. It is worth mentioning that this study will be further enhanced by an upcoming work that addresses the problem of stability, namely finding bounds on the size of the region surrounding a particular equilibrium state within the system, which is an essential outcome in itself and has important implications for understanding and modeling these systems.

The concept of search term recognition is crucial in concept positioning tasks, which involve generating suitable concepts based on user queries. Most current approaches tackle this challenge without identifying the search terms or assume a predetermined set of terms. Research has shown, however, that incorporating search term recognition can boost concept positioning performance. Despite the significance of this component, search term recognition is infrequently addressed in concept positioning studies and generally relied on manually defined sets of possible search terms. Three key issues stem from this manual approach to search term recognition: first, the need to manually define and align concepts and search terms, a task that becomes increasingly difficult with large datasets; second, the necessity to account for term variations such as synonyms and related concepts; and third, the potential for incorrect search term identification due to contextual differences. We aim to address these problems by developing an automated search term recognition method for concept positioning. Our search term recognition model is based on a retrieval system that aligns candidate search terms with user queries, employing a tailored ranking algorithm to address semantic differences. We evaluate our approach on two concept positioning datasets and compare its performance to baseline methods, finding that our approach outperforms baseline methods on both datasets.

Researchers have discovered a unique phenomenon where an external vibration in colloidal gels reduces their mechanical strength and ability to withstand stress. To further investigate this "rheo-acoustic" effect, the impact of different vibration forces, frequencies, and durations were examined and studied in relation to the rigidity of these gels. By utilizing various techniques, such as testing the gels under stress and observing their structure under a microscope, the transition from solid-like to liquid-like behavior in these gels was monitored over time. The results showed that damaging these gels with ultrasonic waves is a gradual process, where repeated vibrations lead to the formation of internal cracks and reduce their mechanical strength. Additionally, the study found that the rigidity of these gels can be restored over time after the vibrations cease. To further understand this phenomenon, the study simulated various scenarios of real-world applications where these gels are exposed to external forces and changed their shape and structure under different conditions, leading to the reorganization of particles in these gels through mechanical stress. The study's findings provide new insights into the behavior of these gels under different forces and can potentially lead to the development of new technologies that utilize ultrasonic waves to manipulate and modify gel structures.

The Collatz Conjecture is a well-known hypothesis dating back to the 1930s, 
stating that for any arbitrary positive integer, alternating between dividing by 3 and dividing by 2 (with allowance for a multiplication by 1) and then taking the integer's absolute value will eventually yield 1 after a certain number of iterations. Despite being unproven for over 80 years, researchers have consistently explored the problem through both analytical methods and computer simulations. This research paper will cover the Collatz Conjecture in detail, involving its origins, variations, and most recent findings as of March 2021.

To effectively classify STEM documents, it's necessary to understand their category, which requires analyzing both technical and categorization-specific content. Both human-written papers and machine-generated texts, such as mathematical articles, utilize mathematical notations to convey complex concepts, making category classification challenging due to the inherent difficulties. Prior approaches to this problem rely heavily on full references, which are not always available, and use insufficient methods of document categorization. To address this issue, we investigated how mathematical entities relate to categories in STEM documents, as their presence provides clues about document categories, and we developed a model utilizing categorical embeddings to represent documents' underlying characteristics. This research sets the stage for our proposed categorization model, which will be presented in the accompanying paper.

The performance of matching methods like kernel regression and support vector prediction in call and kidney transplant data when simulated with the actual underlying distribution is evaluated for their prediction accuracy. We find that using a small number of randomly selected data points, chosen based on their proximity to the query point as estimated by their covariance matrices, yields superior results compared to using the full dataset. We believe this approach can effectively leverage large datasets without requiring computationally expensive pre-processing steps.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are limited in their effectiveness,
primarily focusing on either coherence or similarity with reference summaries.
As an alternative, we introduce SummScore, a versatile metric that utilizes a Cross-Encoder
to comprehensively evaluate summarization performance across various assessment dimensions.
Our research demonstrates the benefits of SummScore in comparable learning and its general applicability
to practical summarization assessment. Additionally, we investigate the underlying challenges
associated with existing summary evaluation metrics at scale and propose Cross-Encoder-based
solutions to improve robustness and fairness. Our findings and associated code are publicly accessible.

The recovery rate of signal recovery algorithms can significantly improve when applying quadratic measurements. In this paper, we investigate the minimum number of quadratic measurements required for complete signal recovery through semidefinite programming (SDP). First, we will focus on a specific type of sparse signal recovery and establish an upper limit for the required quadratic measurements. Next, we will use this bound as a standard to develop a general formula for the minimum number of quadratic measurements needed for recovering any signal. Our proposed formula is then compared with an existing optimal formula by Tropp using Lloyd's maximum correlation criterion. Lastly, we will verify the effectiveness of our formula through numerical experiments conducted using various types of signals.

The widespread use of LiDAR cameras in robotics and computer vision has led to the development of several fusion methods, albeit many of them are still unclear about their internal working processes. This lack of transparency complicates the selection of an efficient and robust feature representation for specific tasks. To tackle this issue, we introduce B Efusion: a simple yet effective random feature learning framework that combines LiDAR and camera data. To train our method, we created a simulated 3D environment to generate pairs of real 3D and real image datasets. We test our approach on navigating indoor spaces by establishing a navigation task, where a robot is tasked with avoiding obstacles to reach targets using features derived from our method. Compared to existing approaches, our method requires less computational effort and achieves comparable performance, if not superior results, under various scene complexities.

In thermal instability of neutral gases, the development of small-scale turbulence near the unstable layer plays a significant role in facilitating heat transfer through convection. The enhanced turbulence increases the exchange rate of heat between the atmosphere and the fluid near the surface, thereby affecting various atmospheric processes. The behavior of dissipation-range liquid turbulence in this context is particularly crucial because it directly influences the rate of heat transfer by modifying the temperature gradient in the fluid. However, accurately modeling this turbulence is a complex task, especially since it often occurs in environments where the fluid flows at very low speeds, thereby avoiding the development of typical instabilities found in fluids. The identification of two distinct types of disturbances that arise due to thermal motions and have different timescales is significant in this context. The long-wave disturbances do not significantly affect the temperature gradient, whereas the short-wave disturbances contribute directly to the temperature fluctuations. The presence of these short-wave disturbances implies that the temperature fluctuations follow a Gaussian distribution, thereby facilitating modeling of the turbulence. The thermal motions can be represented by the energy spectrum of the disturbances, thereby enabling the development of a model that incorporates the effects of thermal disturbances and facilitates numerical simulations. The results suggest that thermal motions do not adversely affect the velocity structure of the fluid and instead modify the temperature fluctuations and the temperature variance in accordance with a predetermined timescale. The effects of thermal motions on the temperature variance exhibit power-law behavior and the variance displays self-similar behavior throughout the simulation.

We have developed an accurate numerical solution to the heat equation, taking into account the unique properties of the liquid as well as the energy transferred by the laser. The simulation reveals that thermal diffusion occurs faster than the propagation of the laser intensity, which is typically assumed in simplified models. The data shows that temperature fluctuations are primarily driven by the laser's intensity gradients rather than its actual energy absorption. The experimentally observed unusual diffraction patterns are largely the result of these intense heat flux angles. Furthermore, we have found that temperature stratification significantly impacts the laser's power distribution, which is more substantial than in cases where the heat equation's assumption of uniform density is applied. The study also shows that temperature-induced refractive index changes mainly affect self-steering patterns by altering phase matching and the critical angle of total internal reflection. It is essential to consider these effects when modeling non-linear propagation in optically dense media.

To enhance end user equipment, the mining of usage data plays a crucial role in guiding design decisions. With the rise of natural language-based interfaces, mining designer's design dialogues presents an opportunity to gain valuable insights into designer's thought process, which can be used to refine design and create more user-friendly products. This paper focuses on the design dialogue mining and its link to mining end user usage data. We aim to provide a well-defined dataset for researchers to better understand the end user experience and make more informed design choices. Additionally, we establish that mining designer's design dialogues has the potential to greatly impact mining end user usage data and future design practices. We demonstrate this through a case study on a voice interface design, highlighting and explaining design choices made by designers. We use human assessment to evaluate the impact of these design choices on user experience and future design practices. We conduct an experiment to assess the impact of these design choices on user experience and future design practices. We conclude that design robustness is crucial for designing product features, including voice interfaces. We provide recommendations for designers to ensure the design features are stable and consistent in order to greatly improve user experience.

The prevailing approach for processing evolving data employs distributed stream processing frameworks, treating the stream as a permanent entity that only exists momentarily. In contrast, we propose a new stream processing paradigm that treats the stream as an integral part of an ever-shifting landscape of data. This approach, built upon temporary and permanent data storage components, enables the efficient processing of both streaming data and its historical context. This work presents a prototype system, called H-STREAM, that incorporates the proposed paradigm. Additionally, we illustrate in a pipeline-based query language how to leverage this architecture for performing analytical tasks, demonstrating its capabilities through a case study leveraging Twitter data. Further information is available online at http://diwaltz.github.io/H-STREAM/.

A thorough analysis of comprehensive generation forests for top- and bottom-associated symbols is presented, extending prior research that focused on top-associates alone. New, non-resonant forests specifically designed for single-generation structures are introduced, allowing for direct manipulation and analysis. Key properties, including diversity, coverage, and calibration, are explicitly determined for bottom-associates, and a novel measurement, coverage-standardized diversity, is used to compare generation methods. By merging top- and bottom-associate forests, coverage-standardized diversity is found to improve by at least 22.8% on average, and generation performance is shown to be calibrated when the number of samples equals the population size. Furthermore, the proposed generation method is found to be versatile, applicable not only to symbolic AI but also across various areas of probabilistic machine learning.

In neural machine translation, a specific system known as the encoder-decoder model with attention has yielded superior results. However, recent studies have attempted to replicate this success in other domains, such as knowledge base translation. A knowledge base translation system resembles a machine that copies information from one language to another, with the ability to learn relevant components of each sentence. Despite some models achieving this task with conditional encoding, our analysis suggests that these models overlook essential aspects of each sentence. To address this limitation, we developed a novel approach that allows a knowledge base translation system to selectively learn and retain unique, dual-purpose components from each language. By leveraging this approach in our SPARQL neural machine translation framework, we outperform existing models when evaluating SPARQL sentence translation using the existing training and testing datasets.

When evaluating the quality of a publication, two key factors are often considered: 
the conference or journal where it was published and the publication's impact factor. 
However, studies have shown that these metrics have significant limitations. To address this, 
I propose relying more on what I term "venue metrics" such as the reputation of the published conference or journal, 
the publication's ranking within its field, and the number of high-quality publications the conference or journal accepts. 
Experiments have revealed that by incorporating these four metrics, we can accurately substitute for citation-based metrics in predicting a publication's quality. 
Furthermore, incorporating these metrics in conjunction with human assessment can identify top publications more effectively than relying on citations alone.

As a crucial part in the overall control system design, the assessment of control software plays a significant role in ensuring performance and ensuring the system functions correctly. This study provides a comprehensive review of the verification and validation of learning-based controllers in autonomous vehicles, focusing on their use in predicting the behavior of neural networks. It aims to identify and categorize the existing approaches, highlighting both the benefits and limitations of each method, as well as suggesting potential future directions to explore.

Graph algorithms for clustering typically offer various functionalities but lack a key aspect in applying these clumps to external data sets due to a limitation in being non-functional. We introduce a novel grouping technique named PHGO that addresses this issue by incorporating a unified framework combining node and edge importance measures. This technique dynamically creates a multi-layered graph where nodes represent individual data points and edges their shared overlaps. Subsequently, a modified version of the lexicographic sweep algorithm is utilized to identify clumps while preserving the inherent structure of the input data. The described method has been successfully applied and evaluated on image data, protein alignments, and gene expressions for their capability in creating informative visualizations and organizing data in an organized structure. Furthermore, a comprehensive demonstration is provided to illustrate the functional nature of PHGO.

In this research, we introduce a new, real-time method for recovering damaged tensor ring signals from incomplete data. By leveraging a moving patch window, our algorithm iteratively refines its estimation and updates the recovered tensor ring for every new input. The main contributions of our approach are threefold: Firstly, we incorporate a patch-based monitoring system to continuously assess the quality of the estimated tensor ring within the moving window. This adaptive mechanism ensures consistent and reliable updates. Secondly, we design a streaming tensor ring restoration algorithm that effectively combines outdated and fresh information within the window. By concurrently optimizing the two parts of the estimate, we achieve optimal results. Lastly, our method utilizes a streamlined initialization procedure that effectively balances the recovery performance and the speed of the algorithm, using a pre-optimized tensor ring and an adaptive solver. We thoroughly test our approach, demonstrating its superiority to existing techniques through comprehensive experiments with synthetic and real-world images.

It is demonstrated that with the exception of four exceptional cases, a Nichols algebra over a Weyl group's root lattice root system can be freely generated by quasisymmetries. The exceptional cases correspond to the groups $G_2\times G_2$, $2A_n$ and $n\geq 3$, $A_l\times A_k$ with $l, k\geq 4$.

This work investigates the inertial wave turbulence within a rotating sphere, employing direct numerical simulations and large eddy simulations to determine the spectrum of the vorticity magnitude. Utilizing the torus geometry, we generate a highly non-reciprocal medium in which to simulate turbulence that is intrinsically anisotropic and far from equilibrium, mimicking the behavior of turbulence in astrophysical and geochemical environments. By conducting over one hundred high-resolution simulations, we identify the inertial wave turbulence spectrum as $E_{\zeta}(\mathbf{k},\phi)$ being proportional to $|\mathbf{k}|^{-2}$ for the specific case of a rotating sphere, validating the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum within predetermined accuracy limits. Furthermore, we find that the vorticity's statistical distribution is composed of a combination of two distinct exponential components. These findings are particular to the simulated astrophysical and geochemical systems. Note that the term "proportional to" indicates a relationship held true except possibly at a finite number of points.

The iterative graph normalization method known as the Leiden algorithm combines multiple techniques to produce a balanced and community-structured network. A key underlying assumption is that the algorithm's output is consistent, yet recent studies have demonstrated significant variations in output depending on starting conditions. Furthermore, these studies have shown that understanding the algorithm's behavior is crucial for analyzing the algorithm itself. This realization led to the study of how the algorithm transforms the graph when operating on distinct areas of the graph. Additionally, these studies have shown that understanding how the algorithm affects different parts of the graph leads to important consequences for studying complex networks. This research is further developing relationships between the algorithm's output and key network characteristics, using a specific example based on a special type of set with maximal weight within it. This example has broader implications for understanding how the algorithm affects distinct network components.

A comprehensive analysis is provided for the thermodynamic properties of a monolayer graphene that electrowears a ferromagnetic atom. This analysis includes standing electron wave function and energy calculations for the system's electrons as well as various key parameters such as the Heisenberg principle, the work done by the electric field, and the electron entropy. Additionally, the findings highlight the influence of the electric field on the electron's entropy and the behavior of the electrons in the graphene's band. A distinction is also made regarding the sub-lattice symmetry of the electron's density in the presence of the electric field.

Recent observations of the CR Draconis system, a close binary system involving M3.5/M6 stars, have continued to document low-frequency radio activity associated with its flares. Over a nearly two decade period, multiple radio telescopes such as the Very Large Array and the Green Bank Telescope have detected numerous episodes of low-frequency radio emission in the system, often lasting days. These radio emission episodes, often strongest at specific frequencies, exhibit rapid increases and decreases in intensity similar to other active binary systems, such as the \alpha Andromedae system, suggesting the presence of a gyro-surface process via beam formation and acceleration theory. Furthermore, the similar characteristics of its radio emission patterns to that of spectro-polarimetric observations of solar flares support the hypothesis of magnetospheric radiation of origin through electron-cyclotron maser instability.

Achieving photorealistic representation of human-like characters in 3D space remains a challenging task, particularly with the added complexity of articulation. To effectively visualize these avatars, 3D representations are essential for seamless navigation and enhanced understanding. However, conventional 2D and 3D rendering methods fall short by compromising between appearance and articulation. To address this issue, a novel framework called ANR is presented, enabling fast and flexible generation of customized images from multiple views through a multi-stage pipeline. Distinct from conventional rendering techniques, ANR utilizes neural networks to achieve real-time creation of tailored textures and colors from input views, including environmental influences. Furthermore, ANR allows for the creation of customizable products with minimal data required, thanks to its ability to extract essential parameters from a few reference images. The ANR framework also includes tools for combining multiple artistic styles and optimizing results, leading to realistic and articulately-driven images.

The ability to perform "image altering" tasks is a crucial image processing capability, essential for tasks like removing digital noise and enhancing image quality for visually impaired individuals.  Evaluating how images are altered by image processing techniques involves both subjective and objective analyses.  Subjective image evaluation is conducted by presenting the image alterations to humans, either professionally trained or not, to determine their perceptive impact.  Objective evaluation, on the other hand, involves analyzing images mathematically to quantify their similarity or divergence.  By comparing these two approaches, we often underestimate the effect an image processing technique has on a image by relying solely on subjective or objective measures.  By presenting the image alterations resulting from intense, severe, or extreme processing techniques, humans respond differently than expected when the results are merely presented numerically by algorithms, despite these techniques having the same objective effect on image analysis.  This discrepancy occurs, as it's discovered that image alterations resulting from intense processing techniques have complex visual patterns that over- or under-emphasize specific image features, causing a unique response from humans.  This unique response can also be observed in deep neural networks, an area where research has been previously limited to natural, generic test patterns, but is now proven to be highly dependent on the specific image alterations resulting from intense processing techniques, having a considerable impact on a variety of image analysis applications.

Under a bosonic realization of the Askey-Wilson algebra, different representations of this algebra correspond to various stages of the exponential of a Lie algebra nilpotent orbit, which are unified by a common anti-involution. Furthermore, this property is extended to a broader context of the link symbol calculus within the context of Chern-Simons theory.

The computational study of a strongly frustrated trimer antiferromagnet on an open honeycomb lattice at low temperatures Trimer-H is conducted using the cluster quantum Monte Carlo method. Our research finds that as the coupling strength between adjacent trimer units (J') increases, the material transforms from a weakly-coupled two-dimensional (2D) network into a one-dimensional (1D) highly-coupled system. We confirm that Trimer-H features a level crossing related to a sign change in the ground state's wave function at a specific point (point C) at approximately J'/J = 0.16. Our results also indicate the ground state's insulating behavior in all studied regions. Moreover, the material exhibits an intrinsic 2D characteristics in the weakly-coupled regime up to a strength of J' approximately equal to 0.18. As such, the material cannot be classified as a true 1D highly-coupled system even in this weakly-coupled regime. Our research utilizes the quantum Einstein relation to evaluate the experimental validity of the previously reported first-order phase transition at point C. Our research finds that the speed at which the dimer correlation decreases is extremely high at point C and contradicts the prediction of a first-order phase transition. As such, the phase transition at point C is likely a continuous change rather than a sudden one.

Recent advancements in open-domain question-answering technologies provide new possibilities for learning systems to acquire knowledge automatically from extensive datasets. Typically, these systems rely on heuristics like choosing the most applicable answers based on the question's natural language description. The question is then refined and another relevant answer is selected. We've compiled a collection of 50 diverse datasets expressed in the same way as the questions, along with their corresponding descriptions. The descriptions provide crucial information about the answers, yet this knowledge is not applied properly by current language models. We've found that the issue is not due to a lack of capacity, but rather a failure to effectively utilize the description when choosing an answer. By fine-tuning the language models on both the description and answer collections, we've significantly improved their ability to learn new knowledge from these datasets, resulting in superior performance on newly collected datasets. The models we've developed achieve state-of-the-art results on recently introduced large-scale zero-shot learning datasets such as PREDICT and PREDICT-IE.

We explore an electroweak phase shift within the framework of a specific three-generation variant of the NMSSM that's resistant to $Z_3$ symmetrization. This particular model is particularly well-suited for examining the focus of our research: corrections to the electroweak parameter $\Delta\rw$, as well as its implications for stabilizing dark matter under the $Z_3$ symmetry, and potential signs of new physics observable at the LHC and in the cosmic sphere. In the LHC context, we concentrate on one of the absolute values of Higgs boson couplings to electrons and bottom quarks; in the cosmic realm, on the production of gravitational waves by such an inflationary model drawn from our research, focusing on the primordial stochastic background of these waves and its properties.

Photometric response function (PRF) measurements are critical for calculating optical depth in spectroscopic studies of the CO line at z > 6. However, current PRF data are insufficient for this purpose. Analyzing the CO line at these high redshifts requires at least three well-constrained PRF points. To address this issue, we developed a new method, the high-z PRF search or hz-PRF, to detect robust redshifts in the range of 6 to 10 using millimeter and submillimeter data. This approach, which incorporates clumpfind, focuses on identifying robust redshifts in the data. Using our hz-PRF on mock line data at different redshifts, we evaluated the method's effectiveness. The results from these mock line data analyses reveal that the hz-PRF efficiently identifies robust redshifts in the data. This approach then applies to various real lines, such as those in ABSMSS J133257.3-012505, and verifies if they can be accurately modeled using existing redshifts. The hz-PRF is now available as a interactive tool on the Python package pycundee, which includes the analysis of ABSMSJ133257.3-012505. This new method is the first to systematically analyze millimeter and submillimeter data at these high redshifts. The hz-PRF is also the first to detect robust (sub)mm shifts in

To determine the actual ground state of the hole-doped antiferromagnetic parent compound of cuprates in the experimentally accessible range of doping, the dynamic structural and magnetic properties of the doped antiferromagnetic semiconductor and the proposed symmetry-conserving and disrupting ordered states are investigated using the Monte Carlo method in the 2D Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice. Our results demonstrate that the broken symmetry state generates structural fluctuations in accordance with the predictions of the structural Goldstone mode theory, whereas the dynamical structural data actually reveals a pattern consistent with the liquid phase with no distinct goldstone modes evident at finite temperatures. Additionally, the broken symmetry and liquid phases yield distinct magnetic behavior, specifically in the presence of a magnetic field, where the former exhibits a field-induced spin wave spectrum in line with the Yafet-K assassin formula and the latter exhibits a dip in the spin excitations consistent with the predictions of the liquid phase within a field-quenched mean-field theory. Our findings suggest that the broken symmetry and liquid phases can be distinguished through measurements of the dynamic structural and magnetic properties and that the latter is more accessible with advanced neutron spectroscopy.

Our SU(3) gauge theory includes a complex triplet Higgs field with free boundary conditions in three dimensions. The model features two phases characterized by the Higgs field's non-zero expectation values in specific directions. As the Higgs field's self-interaction strength varies, these phases are separated by a transitional point. To analyze the deconfined phase with a non-zero expectation value in only one direction, we employ the renormalization group method and determine the critical exponent of the 2-loop model, which is 0.2342 for the 6-dimensional Einstein action and 0.1871 for the 3-dimensional Lattice action. Additionally, we calculate critical exponents for the model with a zero boundary condition, which has three possible orientations for the Higgs field. The results show that all three phases exhibit similar behavior as the underlying theory varies from QED to SU(6) gauge theory. The renormalization group method yields the following critical exponents: for the 2-loop model with a zero boundary condition, we have ω magnetization = 0.5, ω energy = 1.5, and ω correlation length = 2, and for the 5-2 loop model, we have ω correlation length = 1.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits an antiferromagnetic arrangement similar to the L1$_0$ FeAl structure with a N\'eel temperature of 655 K. The in-plane magnetic arrangement is found to consist of a gapless spin wave spectrum. Exchange interactions were determined using the spin wave density of states and magnetic susceptibility data. These results were confirmed through the solution of the classical Heisenberg model for the 2$\times$2 square lattice. However, the exchange interaction between neighboring Al atoms could not be established due to the absence of magnetic moments. The magnetic structure of Cr$_2$Al can be described using the in-plane model with interaction parameters: J$_{1}$ = 16.2 meV and J$_{1\perp}$ = 2.6 meV. The latter is significantly weaker than those found in other 3$d$ transition metal aluminum compounds, contributing to a lower total magnetic energy compared to ferromagnetic arrangements. Consequently, Cr$_2$Al remains unmagnetized and loses its magnetic characteristics at room temperature.

A new model for rarefied gas dynamics, known as the speed-dependent model, is created by modifying the Boltzmann equation's collision term to incorporate variable collision frequencies that conform to experimentally determined values and those derived from the correct cross sections. In particular, it considers the varying interaction forces between molecules as it measures velocity, similar to the method used in Monte Carlo simulations. By comparing numerical outcomes with experimental data and other established methods, it shows that this simple model can accurately depict rarefied gas phenomena where size, pressure, and other factors come into play. Further research indicates that this model can also be used to assess experimentally and computationally challenging properties such as thermal conductivity and heat flux within rarefied gas conditions.

Deep neural networks are highly skilled language interpreters but often lack
understanding of the world. Our proposed solution, the LSAN, injects prior
knowledge into its training, enabling it to accurately translate words into
meaningful concepts like 'animal' and its associated images, with minimal
dependence on extensive datasets. This innovative model relies on an unusual
setup where the analyzer is pre-trained on a unique 'tokenized' language
created from a vast dataset containing single-word images, allowing LSAN to
inculate world knowledge directly into its structure. LSAN is trained solely
by comparing the network's generated meaning representations to these singular
images through contrastive learning, resulting in remarkable performance on a
range of challenging semantic reasoning tasks. This unique approach effectively
bridges the significant gap between current deep models and human-like
understanding, offering new insights to researchers and practitioners.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To determine the quark and gluon distribution functions with high precision and accuracy at all momentum scales, advanced technology, specifically Cherenkov detectors, will be utilized for tracking, particularly in the experiment's detector setup. Cherenkov devices bring about a breakthrough over conventional silicon sensors by enabling spatial resolution independent of momentum in the entire detector coverage, thus enabling the tracing of heavy, high-momentum particles produced in collisions with heavy nuclei. This development enables the tracing of heavy, high-momentum particles produced in collisions with heavy nuclei. This capability will be showcased in a customized Cherenkov-based module for the electron-iron collisions, demonstrating its capability to identify iron jet production in interactions with low energy electrons.

A newly identified, low-power active galactic nucleus in the galaxy NGC 2115, which is classified as an Low EXtreme Active Galaxy (L.EAG.), exhibits significant light fluctuations that switch between high and low levels multiple times over the course of about 514 days. These light fluctuations are detected through unfiltered optical band photometry and have a significant time interval of about 514 days. In addition, the light curve shows further fluctuations with a shorter time interval of about 14.5 days for its secondary component. We have analyzed the optical light produced by the nucleus at its peak and found it to be about 100 times brighter than its quiescent state, which is comparable to the brightness of a large star. This is in contrast to the typical behavior of active galactic nuclei (AGN), where the optical light remains constant at its active galactic nucleus (AGN) peak by comparing it to the brightness of a large star. In order to study the optical behavior of AGN we have obtained spectroscopic data from IUE. Our findings from the Wu-IUE Extragalactic Database (WIDE) reveal that the optical spectrum of NGC 2115 does not contain any prominent emission lines or marks, which indicates that it does not belong in any specific active galactic nucleus (AGN) subcategory. To study the properties of plasma in the star HD58260, we obtained high-resolution spectropolarimetry using the POLIS device on the German VLT, varying the orientation of its electron beam to either 0 or 180 degrees relative to the star's center. This approach allowed us to analyze the star's spectral lines under both natural and instrumental polarization, enabling us to make precise measurements of its magnetic field and polarization properties. As a result, our observations revealed significant differences in the star's magnetic field orientation measured during the electron beam's different phases, showing an impressive immediately. Furthermore, these measurements largely confirm previous studies on the star's circular polarization properties, its average filled degree, and e-folding time for magnetic field decay. Notably, however, the measured parameters exhibited some variation, and these discrepancies from the established values are under close examination to determine their significance.

The analysis reveals an expression in terms of free fields that represents the one-dimensional Dunkl operator with respect to the space of Calderon-Laguerre polynomials, exploiting free field calculus over the real line. This operator's action can be analyzed using a jump process on the half-line and two independent positive half-axis, characterized by a regular transformation of one dimension. In the process, the operator is shown to be positive definite under specific conditions involving its kernel and the underlying Gaussian measure. To facilitate the analysis, the method involves the representation of the Dunkl operator as a product of two operators, one defined over the half-axis and the other defined over the two axis, using the principle of separation of variables. This approach extends existing results from even Calderon-Laguerre polynomials to the broader class of polynomials by removing the even index constraint. Furthermore, the operator's integral representation is derived in conjunction with its generating function, thereby providing a free field representation of the operator with explicit Fourier kernel, thereby establishing an integral operator equivalent to the differential operator. This equivalence forms the basis for a new representation of the operator as an elliptic differential operator with singular coefficients.

A deep atomic hydrogen map of the center of NGC 5253 obtained using ALMA was analyzed. The observed 21 cm line brightness temperature was found to be comparable to that of a young stellar population's photoionized gas in terms of its metal content. Further analysis of the hydrogen layer revealed a large, flat plateau with a uniform temperature of around 21K and also a hotter, thinner layer close to the center of the galaxy with a maximum temperature of around 90K. The width of the hotter, thinner layer that contains most of the total derived column density was estimated. Using an updated ATC model and incorporating both the high and low temperature regions, the total molecular hydrogen content of the center of NGC 5253 was calculated. The efficiency of two processes that form molecular hydrogen from the center of NGC 5253 were then estimated. The conclusions drawn from the 21 cm line observations were also applicable to the 30 GHz H30$\alpha$ line observations which have lower sensitivities than the 21 cm line observations. Using the ATC model and incorporating both the hot and cold regions, the total molecular hydrogen content of the center of NGC 5253 was calculated at different molecular hydrogen contents. The efficiency of two processes that form molecular hydrogen from the center of NGC 5253 were estimated. We define a new concept called continuous orbit similarity rigidity. Let G be a virtually cyclic group and T a G-action on a compact metric space that has rigidity properties. For two orbits i, j the orbit similarity index is calculated as the smallest scale factor s that closely maps the i-th to the j-th orbit. The group G acts on the space through its elements g, where the orbit of i is transformed by g into the j-th orbit. The number s( g, i, j) represents this scaling factor. The collection of these scaling factors for each group element g forms a function called s( g, I, J). When the group element g and orbits i, j are clear from context, we use the notation s( I, J) to denote this function. Our results show that under specific conditions, when the group G is virtually cyclic and the space T is a compact metric space with a rigidity property, then a nearby continuous function s* approximating s( I, J) exists. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions for rigidity, along with sufficient conditions for the approximate function s* to be continuous, as well as for the equivalence of several expressions involving s*. Our method also enables generalizations to a broader class of groups, including surface groups, and non-finitely generated groups, while we also provide applications in computation of stable invariants of orbits in maps with a G-symmetry.
